entries.quoted_span:
The maximum-security deposit to be collected by the landlord cannot be more than 
one and one-half times one month’s rent ( N.J.S.A. 46:8-21.2 ).

entries.explanation: Applies. Landlords cannot charge more than $50 (adjusted for inflation) to apply for a rental, except in one- or two-family homes (Statewide rule: N.J.S.A. 46:8-18.1). entries.requirement: A landlord or agent may not require an application or similar fee to apply to lease or sublease a residential rental property that exceeds $50, adjusted annually for CPI increases. Violators face penalties of up to $500 (first), $750 (second) and $1,000 (subsequent offenses), and the amount wrongfully charged is remitted to the applicant.

A landlord, or
agent thereof, shall not require an application or other similar fee to apply

entries.explanation: Applies. Landlords cannot ask about or use an applicant's criminal record until after a conditional offer, and then only limited convictions with an individual review (Statewide rule: N.J.S.A. 46:8-52 et seq.).  Parcel data: at least 5 units. Exemptions ruled out by that data: Owner-occupied premises of not more than four units.
entries.title: NJ Fair Chance in Housing Act
entries.requirement: Housing providers may not ask about or consider an applicant's criminal record before making a conditional offer. After a conditional offer, only certain convictions within set look-back periods may be considered, subject to an individualized assessment, written notice of withdrawal, and an appeal opportunity. Providers also may not require drug or alcohol tests of applicants.

entries.quoted_span:
A housing
provider
shall not make any oral or written inquiry

entries.explanation: Applies. entries.quoted_span: No landlord shall bring any action to recover possession of a dwelling unit as a reprisal for the tenant's efforts to secure or enforce any right under this chapter.

entries.explanation: Applies. entries.requirement: A landlord may not demand or receive security exceeding one month's rent (two months' rent for small natural-person landlords owning no more than two properties with four units total, except when the tenant is a service member), and must return the deposit with an itemized statement within 21 calendar days after the tenant vacates. Security cannot be labeled nonrefundable, and bad-faith retention can bring statutory damages of up to twice the deposit.
entries.key_value: One month's rent cap (two months for small landlords); 21-day return deadline
entries.quoted_span: a landlord shall not demand or receive security, however denominated, in an amount or value in excess of an amount equal to one month’s rent, in addition to any rent for the first month paid on or before initial occupancy.

entries.explanation: Applies. Landlords can charge only actual screening costs, never over $30 (adjusted for inflation), and must give an itemized receipt (Statewide rule: Cal. Civ. Code § 1950.6). No building-based coverage test applies.
entries.title: California application screening fee limits
entries.requirement: A landlord may charge an application screening fee only up to actual out-of-pocket costs and the reasonable value of time spent, never more than $30 per applicant (adjustable annually with CPI since 1998), and may not charge it when no unit is or will soon be available. The landlord must either consider applications in order and approve the first qualified applicant (charging only when an application is actually considered), or refund the full fee within 7 days of selecting a tenant or 30 days of application, whichever is first; an itemized receipt is required.
entries.key_value: $30 per applicant, CPI-adjusted; itemized receipt required
entries.quoted_span: In no case shall the amount of the application screening fee charged by the landlord or their agent be greater than thirty dollars ($30) per applicant.

entries.explanation: Applies. Landlords cannot discriminate against applicants or tenants because of their income source, including housing vouchers (Statewide rule: California Fair Employment and Housing Act (FEHA); Cal. Gov. Code § 12955). No building-based coverage test applies.
entries.title: California FEHA housing screening limits
entries.citation: California Fair Employment and Housing Act (FEHA); Cal. Gov. Code § 12955
entries.requirement: Owners may not discriminate against or harass a person because of source of income (including Section 8 and HUD-VASH vouchers and other public assistance). Where a government rent subsidy applies, income standards must be based on the tenant's share of rent, and applicants must be allowed to offer alternative evidence of ability to pay instead of credit history; owners may still ask about the level or source of income.
entries.key_value: Source of income protected; subsidy-based income test uses tenant's portion of rent
entries.quoted_span: For the owner of any housing accommodation to discriminate against or harass any person because of the race, color, religion, sex, gender, gender identity, gender expression, sexual orientation, marital status, national origin, ancestry, familial status, source of income,

entries.title: Berkeley relocation assistance for owner move-in and Ellis Act evictions

entries.requirement: Owners must pay tenants relocation assistance when evicting for an owner move-in or to withdraw a unit from the rental market under the Ellis Act. The payment amounts are indexed to inflation and adjusted each year by the Rent Board.

entries.quoted_span: The Rent Stabilization and Good Cause for Eviction Ordinance requires owners to pay tenants relocation assistance in the event of an owner move-in eviction.

entries.explanation: Applies. Berkeley landlords must disclose tenant screening fee rights and the state fee cap, and cannot charge non-refundable renewal or roommate-change fees (Berkeley, CA rule: Berkeley Municipal Code ch. 13.78). No building-based coverage test applies.

entries.requirement: Owners charging a fee for a credit report or application processing must provide a clear tenant screening fee rights statement and the state maximum fee cap before receiving the fee. entries.explanation: Applies. Berkeley landlords cannot ask about or use criminal history in choosing or managing tenants, and must give written notice and a chance to respond first (Berkeley, CA rule: Berkeley Municipal Code ch. 13.106). entries.key_value: Criminal history inquiries and use prohibited; fines $1,000-$10,000 per violation

entries.explanation: Applies. In Berkeley, landlords cannot use pricing software that relies on competitors' private data to set rents, with fines up to $1,000 per violation (Berkeley, CA rule: Berkeley Municipal Code ch. 13.63). No building-based coverage test applies.
entries.title: Berkeley ban on coordinated rent-pricing algorithms
entries.requirement: It is unlawful to sell, license, or provide to Berkeley landlords, or for a landlord to use, a coordinated pricing algorithm that uses non-public competitor data to set or recommend rents or occupancy levels for residential units. entries.key_value: Ban on coordinated pricing algorithms; civil penalties up to $1,000 per violation
entries.quoted_span:
It shall be unlawful for a landlord to use a coordinated pricing algorithm described 
in subsection A when setting rents or occupancy levels for residential dwelling units in 
the City of Berkeley.

entries.requirement: An owner may not raise the gross rental rate over any 12-month period by more than 5 percent plus the local percentage change in the cost of living, or 10 percent, whichever is lower, and may not raise rent more than twice in 12 months for the same tenant. entries.explanation: Applies. New Jersey has no statewide rent control, but towns may adopt their own, and rent increases need proper written notice and cannot be unconscionable (Statewide rule: N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.1 et seq.; N.J.S.A. 2A:42-84.5). No building-based coverage test applies.
entries.title: NJ no state rent control; municipalities may adopt rent control
entries.requirement: The State of New Jersey has no laws that establish, govern or control rents, but municipalities may pass rent control or rent leveling ordinances enforced by local boards. Landlords may raise rent only by proper lease termination and written notice, the increase must not be unconscionable, and it must comply with any municipal rent control ordinance. Newly constructed multiple dwellings are exempt from local rent control for 30 years after completion of construction.
entries.key_value: No state cap; local rent control permitted; new multiple dwellings exempt 30 years
entries.quoted_span:
The State of New Jersey has no laws that establish, govern or control rents. Municipalities 
may pass an ordinance establishing rent control or rent leveling.

entries.explanation: Applies. Landlords can evict or refuse to renew a lease only for specific legal reasons and with a court order, after giving the required written notice (Statewide rule: N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.1 to 61.12).  Parcel data: at least 5 units. Exemptions ruled out by that data: Owner-occupied premises with two or fewer rental units. Not checked from parcel data: the building is not a hotel or motel; unit held in trust for developmentally disabled family member.
entries.title: NJ Anti-Eviction Act
entries.requirement: A residential landlord may remove a tenant or refuse to renew a lease only for a statutory good cause and through a court judgment for possession. Each cause except nonpayment requires a written Notice to Quit with a cause-specific period (3 days to 3 years), some causes need a prior Notice to Cease, and removal for substantial health and safety violations requires relocation assistance first.
entries.key_value: Good cause required; Notice to Quit periods from 3 days up to 3 years depending on cause; relocation assistance of 6 times monthly rent for illegal occupancy evictions
entries.quoted_span:
No residential landlord may evict or fail to renew a 
lease, whether it is a written or an oral lease without good cause.
not_checked: the building is not a hotel or motel
unit held in trust for developmentally disabled family member

entries.explanation: Applies. Landlords cannot collect a security deposit above one and a half months' rent, and yearly increases to the deposit are capped at 10% (Statewide rule: N.J.S.A. 46:8-21.2; N.J.S.A. 46:8-19; N.J.S.A. 46:8-21.1).  Parcel data: at least 5 units. Exemptions ruled out by that data: Owner-occupied two- or three-family dwelling.
entries.title: NJ Security Deposit Law
entries.requirement: A landlord may not collect a security deposit of more than one and one-half times one month's rent, and any yearly increase in the deposit may not exceed 10% of the current deposit. Prepaid rent held as security, including last month's rent, counts toward the cap, and a pet deposit cannot push the total above the cap.
entries.key_value: 1.5 x monthly rent; annual increase max 10% of current deposit
entries.quoted_span:
The maximum-security deposit to be collected by the landlord cannot be more than 
one and one-half times one month’s rent ( N.J.S.A. 46:8-21.2 ).

entries.explanation: Applies. Landlords cannot charge more than $50 (adjusted for inflation) to apply for a rental, except in one- or two-family homes (Statewide rule: N.J.S.A. 46:8-18.1).  Parcel data: at least 5 units. Exemptions ruled out by that data: One- or two-family dwelling. Not checked from parcel data: real estate licensee who is not the landlord (depends on the tenancy).
entries.title: NJ rental application fee cap
entries.requirement: A landlord or agent may not require an application or similar fee to apply to lease or sublease a residential rental property that exceeds $50, adjusted annually for CPI increases. Violators face penalties of up to $500 (first), $750 (second) and $1,000 (subsequent offenses), and the amount wrongfully charged is remitted to the applicant.
entries.key_value: $50 cap (CPI-adjusted annually)
entries.quoted_span:
A landlord, or
agent thereof, shall not require an application or other similar fee to apply
to lease or sublease a residential rental property for dwelling purposes, which
exceeds $50.
not_checked: real estate licensee who is not the landlord (depends on the tenancy)

entries.explanation: Applies. Landlords cannot ask about or use an applicant's criminal record until after a conditional offer, and then only limited convictions with an individual review (Statewide rule: N.J.S.A. 46:8-52 et seq.).  Parcel data: at least 5 units. Exemptions ruled out by that data: Owner-occupied premises of not more than four units.
entries.title: NJ Fair Chance in Housing Act
entries.requirement: Housing providers may not ask about or consider an applicant's criminal record before making a conditional offer. After a conditional offer, only certain convictions within set look-back periods may be considered, subject to an individualized assessment, written notice of withdrawal, and an appeal opportunity. Providers also may not require drug or alcohol tests of applicants.
entries.key_value: No criminal-record inquiry before conditional offer; look-back 6 years (1st degree), 4 years (2nd/3rd degree), 1 year (4th degree); serious listed offenses and lifetime sex-offender registration have no look-back limit
entries.quoted_span:
A housing
provider
shall not make any oral or written inquiry
regarding an applicant’s criminal record prior to making a conditional offer.

entries.explanation: Applies. Landlords cannot refuse to rent because of an applicant's lawful income source, but may still turn down applicants for too little income or bad credit (Statewide rule: N.J.S.A. 10:5-12; New Jersey Law Against Discrimination (N.J.S.A. 10:5-1 et seq.)).  Parcel data: at least 5 units. Exemptions ruled out by that data: Two-family owner-occupied dwelling; Room in owner- or resident-occupied single home.

entries.title: NJ FAIR Act algorithmic rent-setting ban

entries.explanation: Applies. Newark rent increases at lease renewal are limited to the inflation change and never more than 4%, with 30 days' written notice (Newark, NJ rule: Newark Rev. Gen. Ords. ch. 19:2). No building-based coverage test applies. Not checked from parcel data: public housing; the building is not a hotel or motel; the building is not a commercial.
entries.title: Newark Rent Control Ordinance
entries.requirement: At lease expiration or termination of a periodic tenancy, a landlord may not request or receive an increase greater than the CPI percentage change (CPI-U NY-NJ-Long Island, from 15 months prior to 3 months prior to the month of the proposed increase), and in no case more than 4%. Increases are barred if the dwelling is not in substantial compliance or the landlord has not registered, and require 30 days' written notice to the tenant and the Rent Regulation Officer.
entries.key_value: CPI-U change, max 4%
entries.quoted_span: no landlord may request or receive an increase greater than the percentage increase in the Consumer Price Index (CPI) from the CPI 15 months prior to the month of the proposed rent increase to the CPI three months prior to the month of the proposed rent increase. In no case shall the allowable rent increase exceed 4%.

entries.explanation: Applies. Newark defines an unconscionable rent increase as unreasonably harsh, above the landlord's cost increase, and out of line with similar rents (Newark, NJ rule: Newark Municipal Code § 2:10-11.1). No building-based coverage test applies. Not checked from parcel data: exempt from rent control under N.J.S.A. 2A:42-84.1-84.6 or HUD-controlled.
entries.title: Newark unconscionable rent increase ordinance
entries.requirement: Newark defines an 'unconscionable rent' increase for residential rental properties as one that is exceedingly harsh or unreasonable, exceeds the increase in the landlord's expenses, and is not comparable to rents at similar properties. For properties under a redevelopment or financial agreement, rent above the approved pro-forma is per se unconscionable.
entries.key_value: Rent above approved pro-forma is per se unconscionable
entries.quoted_span: Shall mean any rental increase for residential properties including but not limited to market and unsubsidized units, whose rental increases are exceedingly harsh or unreasonable that exceed the increase in the landlord’s expenses; and is not comparable to rents charged at similar properties.

entries.title: Newark retaliatory eviction prohibition

entries.quoted_span: No landlord shall bring any action to recover possession of a dwelling unit as a reprisal for the tenant's efforts to secure or enforce any right under this chapter.

entries.explanation: Applies. New Jersey has no statewide rent control, but towns may adopt their own, and rent increases need proper written notice and cannot be unconscionable (Statewide rule: N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.1 et seq.; N.J.S.A. 2A:42-84.5). No building-based coverage test applies.
entries.title: NJ no state rent control; municipalities may adopt rent control
entries.requirement: The State of New Jersey has no laws that establish, govern or control rents, but municipalities may pass rent control or rent leveling ordinances enforced by local boards. Landlords may raise rent only by proper lease termination and written notice, the increase must not be unconscionable, and it must comply with any municipal rent control ordinance. Newly constructed multiple dwellings are exempt from local rent control for 30 years after completion of construction.
entries.key_value: No state cap; local rent control permitted; new multiple dwellings exempt 30 years
entries.quoted_span:
The State of New Jersey has no laws that establish, govern or control rents. Municipalities 
may pass an ordinance establishing rent control or rent leveling.

entries.title: NJ Anti-Eviction Act
entries.requirement: A residential landlord may remove a tenant or refuse to renew a lease only for a statutory good cause and through a court judgment for possession. Each cause except nonpayment requires a written Notice to Quit with a cause-specific period (3 days to 3 years), some causes need a prior Notice to Cease, and removal for substantial health and safety violations requires relocation assistance first.
entries.key_value: Good cause required; Notice to Quit periods from 3 days up to 3 years depending on cause; relocation assistance of 6 times monthly rent for illegal occupancy evictions
entries.quoted_span:
No residential landlord may evict or fail to renew a 
lease, whether it is a written or an oral lease without good cause.

entries.title: NJ Security Deposit Law

entries.title: California Tenant Protection Act rent cap
entries.requirement: An owner may not raise the gross rental rate over any 12-month period by more than 5 percent plus the local percentage change in the cost of living, or 10 percent, whichever is lower, and may not raise rent more than twice in 12 months for the same tenant. New tenancies (no prior tenant remaining) may start at any rate, and the cap applies only to later increases.

entries.quoted_span: an owner of residential real property shall not, over the course of any 12-month period, increase the gross rental rate for a dwelling or a unit more than 5 percent plus the percentage change in the cost of living, or 10 percent, whichever is lower,

For no-fault terminations the owner must pay one month's rent as relocation assistance within 15 days of notice or waive the final month's rent.

entries.explanation: Applies. Landlords generally cannot take more than one month's rent as a deposit (two for small landlords) and must return it with an itemized list within 21 days (Statewide rule: Cal. Civ. Code § 1950.5). No building-based coverage test applies.
entries.title: California security deposit cap and return rules
entries.requirement: A landlord may not demand or receive security exceeding one month's rent (two months' rent for small natural-person landlords owning no more than two properties with four units total, except when the tenant is a service member), and must return the deposit with an itemized statement within 21 calendar days after the tenant vacates. Security cannot be labeled nonrefundable, and bad-faith retention can bring statutory damages of up to twice the deposit.
entries.key_value: One month's rent cap (two months for small landlords); 21-day return deadline
entries.quoted_span: a landlord shall not demand or receive security, however denominated, in an amount or value in excess of an amount equal to one month’s rent, in addition to any rent for the first month paid on or before initial occupancy.

entries.explanation: Applies. Landlords can charge only actual screening costs, never over $30 (adjusted for inflation), and must give an itemized receipt (Statewide rule: Cal. Civ. Code § 1950.6). No building-based coverage test applies.
entries.title: California application screening fee limits
entries.requirement: A landlord may charge an application screening fee only up to actual out-of-pocket costs and the reasonable value of time spent, never more than $30 per applicant (adjustable annually with CPI since 1998), and may not charge it when no unit is or will soon be available. The landlord must either consider applications in order and approve the first qualified applicant (charging only when an application is actually considered), or refund the full fee within 7 days of selecting a tenant or 30 days of application, whichever is first; an itemized receipt is required.
entries.key_value: $30 per applicant, CPI-adjusted; itemized receipt required
entries.quoted_span: In no case shall the amount of the application screening fee charged by the landlord or their agent be greater than thirty dollars ($30) per applicant.

entries.explanation: Applies. Landlords cannot discriminate against applicants or tenants because of their income source, including housing vouchers (Statewide rule: California Fair Employment and Housing Act (FEHA); Cal. Gov. Code § 12955). No building-based coverage test applies.
entries.title: California FEHA housing screening limits
entries.citation: California Fair Employment and Housing Act (FEHA); Cal. Gov. Code § 12955
entries.requirement: Owners may not discriminate against or harass a person because of source of income (including Section 8 and HUD-VASH vouchers and other public assistance). Where a government rent subsidy applies, income standards must be based on the tenant's share of rent, and applicants must be allowed to offer alternative evidence of ability to pay instead of credit history; owners may still ask about the level or source of income.

entries.explanation: Applies. New Jersey has no statewide rent control, but towns may adopt their own, and rent increases need proper written notice and cannot be unconscionable (Statewide rule: N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.1 et seq.; N.J.S.A. 2A:42-84.5). No building-based coverage test applies.
entries.title: NJ no state rent control; municipalities may adopt rent control
entries.requirement: The State of New Jersey has no laws that establish, govern or control rents, but municipalities may pass rent control or rent leveling ordinances enforced by local boards. Landlords may raise rent only by proper lease termination and written notice, the increase must not be unconscionable, and it must comply with any municipal rent control ordinance. Newly constructed multiple dwellings are exempt from local rent control for 30 years after completion of construction.
entries.key_value: No state cap; local rent control permitted; new multiple dwellings exempt 30 years
entries.quoted_span:
The State of New Jersey has no laws that establish, govern or control rents. Municipalities 
may pass an ordinance establishing rent control or rent leveling.

entries.explanation: Applies. entries.explanation: Applies. A rental broker can work for the tenant or the landlord but not both, and only the party who hired the broker pays the fee (Statewide rule: G.L. c. 112 § 87DDD1/2). No building-based coverage test applies.

entries.explanation: Applies. entries.quoted_span: Under the law, landlords, sellers and rental agents may use any reasonable standard to determine which applicants are selected, as long as that standard is applied equally and uniformly to all applicants.

entries.explanation: Applies. Landlords generally cannot take more than one month's rent as a deposit (two for small landlords) and must return it with an itemized list within 21 days (Statewide rule: Cal. Civ. Code § 1950.5). No building-based coverage test applies.
entries.title: California security deposit cap and return rules
entries.requirement: A landlord may not demand or receive security exceeding one month's rent (two months' rent for small natural-person landlords owning no more than two properties with four units total, except when the tenant is a service member), and must return the deposit with an itemized statement within 21 calendar days after the tenant vacates. Security cannot be labeled nonrefundable, and bad-faith retention can bring statutory damages of up to twice the deposit.
entries.key_value: One month's rent cap (two months for small landlords); 21-day return deadline
entries.quoted_span: a landlord shall not demand or receive security, however denominated, in an amount or value in excess of an amount equal to one month’s rent, in addition to any rent for the first month paid on or before initial occupancy.

entries.explanation: Applies. Landlords can charge only actual screening costs, never over $30 (adjusted for inflation), and must give an itemized receipt (Statewide rule: Cal. Civ. Code § 1950.6). No building-based coverage test applies.
entries.title: California application screening fee limits
entries.requirement: A landlord may charge an application screening fee only up to actual out-of-pocket costs and the reasonable value of time spent, never more than $30 per applicant (adjustable annually with CPI since 1998), and may not charge it when no unit is or will soon be available. The landlord must either consider applications in order and approve the first qualified applicant (charging only when an application is actually considered), or refund the full fee within 7 days of selecting a tenant or 30 days of application, whichever is first; an itemized receipt is required.
entries.key_value: $30 per applicant, CPI-adjusted; itemized receipt required
entries.quoted_span: In no case shall the amount of the application screening fee charged by the landlord or their agent be greater than thirty dollars ($30) per applicant.

entries.explanation: Applies. It is illegal to use or sell shared pricing software built on competitors' data to coordinate prices or force others to follow its prices (Statewide rule: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 16729). No building-based coverage test applies.
entries.title: California common pricing algorithm ban
entries.requirement: It is unlawful to use or distribute a common pricing algorithm, meaning software or other technology used by two or more persons that uses competitor data to recommend, align, set or influence a price, as part of a conspiracy to restrain trade, or to coerce another person to adopt the algorithm's recommended price or term. The text is general and does not name rental housing.
entries.quoted_span: It shall be unlawful for a person to use or distribute a common pricing algorithm as part of a contract, combination in the form of a trust, or conspiracy to restrain trade or commerce in violation of this chapter.

entries.explanation: Applies. New Jersey has no statewide rent control, but towns may adopt their own, and rent increases need proper written notice and cannot be unconscionable (Statewide rule: N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.1 et seq.; N.J.S.A. 2A:42-84.5). No building-based coverage test applies.
entries.title: NJ no state rent control; municipalities may adopt rent control
entries.requirement: The State of New Jersey has no laws that establish, govern or control rents, but municipalities may pass rent control or rent leveling ordinances enforced by local boards. Landlords may raise rent only by proper lease termination and written notice, the increase must not be unconscionable, and it must comply with any municipal rent control ordinance. Newly constructed multiple dwellings are exempt from local rent control for 30 years after completion of construction.
entries.key_value: No state cap; local rent control permitted; new multiple dwellings exempt 30 years
entries.quoted_span:
The State of New Jersey has no laws that establish, govern or control rents. Municipalities 
may pass an ordinance establishing rent control or rent leveling.

entries.explanation: Applies. Landlords can evict or refuse to renew a lease only for specific legal reasons and with a court order, after giving the required written notice (Statewide rule: N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.1 to 61.12).  Parcel data: built 2007, at least 5 units. Exemptions ruled out by that data: Owner-occupied premises with two or fewer rental units. Not checked from parcel data: the building is not a hotel or motel; unit held in trust for developmentally disabled family member.
entries.title: NJ Anti-Eviction Act
entries.requirement: A residential landlord may remove a tenant or refuse to renew a lease only for a statutory good cause and through a court judgment for possession. Each cause except nonpayment requires a written Notice to Quit with a cause-specific period (3 days to 3 years), some causes need a prior Notice to Cease, and removal for substantial health and safety violations requires relocation assistance first.
entries.key_value: Good cause required; Notice to Quit periods from 3 days up to 3 years depending on cause; relocation assistance of 6 times monthly rent for illegal occupancy evictions
entries.quoted_span:
No residential landlord may evict or fail to renew a 
lease, whether it is a written or an oral lease without good cause.

entries.explanation: Applies. Landlords cannot collect a security deposit above one and a half months' rent, and yearly increases to the deposit are capped at 10% (Statewide rule: N.J.S.A. 46:8-21.2; N.J.S.A. 46:8-19; N.J.S.A. 46:8-21.1).  Parcel data: built 2007, at least 5 units. Exemptions ruled out by that data: Owner-occupied two- or three-family dwelling.
entries.title: NJ Security Deposit Law
entries.requirement: A landlord may not collect a security deposit of more than one and one-half times one month's rent, and any yearly increase in the deposit may not exceed 10% of the current deposit. Prepaid rent held as security, including last month's rent, counts toward the cap, and a pet deposit cannot push the total above the cap.

entries.explanation: Applies. Landlords cannot charge more than $50 (adjusted for inflation) to apply for a rental, except in one- or two-family homes (Statewide rule: N.J.S.A. 46:8-18.1). entries.explanation: Applies. entries.explanation: Applies. Boston landlords ending a tenancy must give the tenant a rights and resources notice with the eviction notice and send a copy to the city (Boston, MA rule: Boston City Ordinances § 10-11.7). No building-based coverage test applies. Not checked from parcel data: the building is not a hospital, skilled nursing or health facility; the building is not a short-term substance abuse treatment facility.
entries.title: Boston Housing Stability Notification Act
entries.requirement: A landlord or foreclosing owner ending a tenancy must deliver a Notice of Tenants' Rights and Resources to the tenant at the same time as the Notice to Quit or non-renewal notice, and send a copy of that notice with a Certificate of Compliance/Service to the City's Office of Housing Stability. Violations draw a warning, then $300 per day, but do not halt the eviction process.
entries.key_value: Notice of Tenants' Rights and Resources delivered with Notice to Quit; copy to Office of Housing Stability
entries.quoted_span: The HSNA becomes effective on November 6, 2020.
not_checked: the building is not a hospital, skilled nursing or health facility
the building is not a short-term substance abuse treatment facility

entries.explanation: Unknown. Boston housing providers with city funding or income-restricted units cannot impose blanket criminal bans, use old or non-conviction records, or use credit scores to deny applicants (Boston, MA rule: Boston Fair Chance Tenant Selection Policy (DND, Feb. 2017)). Coverage depends on: requires receives city DND funding or land, or has BPDA inclusionary income-restricted units, which is not in the parcel data.
entries.title: Boston Fair Chance Tenant Selection Policy
entries.citation: Boston Fair Chance Tenant Selection Policy (DND, Feb. 2017)
entries.requirement: Covered housing providers may not impose blanket denials based on arrests or convictions and must not consider non-conviction arrests, judicially relieved convictions, juvenile records, or convictions more than 5 years old (subject to exceptions for direct relationship/unreasonable risk of harm). They also may not use applicants' credit scores to approve or deny applications.
entries.key_value: No blanket bans; no consideration of arrests without conviction, sealed/expunged or juvenile records, or convictions over 5 years old; no credit score use
entries.quoted_span:
will not impose a blanket policy that denies 
housing to anyone with arrests and or convictions. Housing providers will consider applicants on 
a case-by-case basis.

entries.explanation: Applies. Boston landlords cannot discriminate against tenants or applicants who use rental assistance such as Section 8 vouchers (Boston, MA rule: Boston Fair Housing Commission fair housing regulations). No building-based coverage test applies.
entries.title: Boston rental assistance discrimination ban
entries.citation: Boston Fair Housing Commission fair housing regulations
entries.requirement: Landlords in Boston may not discriminate against tenants or applicants because they use rental assistance, including Section 8 vouchers, social security disability vouchers and veterans vouchers. Telling an applicant the landlord does not accept rental assistance is cited as an example of housing discrimination.
entries.key_value: Rental assistance is a protected class
entries.quoted_span:
The landlord tells you they don't accept rental assistance. This includes Section
8 vouchers, social security disability vouchers, and veterans vouchers.

entries.explanation: Applies. Rent increases are capped at 5% plus local inflation, up to 10%, for housing older than 15 years, unless an exemption such as an owner-occupied duplex applies (Statewide rule: Cal. Civ. Code § 1947.12). Built 1990: meets the test (first occupied on or before 2011-10-01). Parcel data: built 1990, 32 units. Exemptions ruled out by that data: Owner-occupied duplex. Not checked from parcel data: restricted affordable housing; the building is not a dormitory; the building is not a separately alienable home or condominium unit.
entries.title: California Tenant Protection Act rent cap
entries.requirement: An owner may not raise the gross rental rate over any 12-month period by more than 5 percent plus the local percentage change in the cost of living, or 10 percent, whichever is lower, and may not raise rent more than twice in 12 months for the same tenant. New tenancies (no prior tenant remaining) may start at any rate, and the cap applies only to later increases.
entries.key_value: 5% + CPI, max 10%
entries.quoted_span: an owner of residential real property shall not, over the course of any 12-month period, increase the gross rental rate for a dwelling or a unit more than 5 percent plus the percentage change in the cost of living, or 10 percent, whichever is lower,

entries.explanation: Superseded. After a tenant has lived in a unit 12 months, the landlord needs a stated legal reason to end the tenancy, and must pay one month's rent for no-fault evictions (Statewide rule: Cal. Civ. Code § 1946.2). Here it gives way to Los Angeles Just Cause for Eviction Ordinance (JCO) (r-0022), which applies at this address.
entries.title: California Tenant Protection Act just cause
entries.requirement: After a tenant has continuously and lawfully occupied a unit for 12 months, the owner may terminate the tenancy only for stated at-fault or no-fault just cause. For no-fault terminations the owner must pay one month's rent as relocation assistance within 15 days of notice or waive the final month's rent.
entries.key_value: Just cause after 12 months' occupancy; no-fault relocation = one month's rent
entries.quoted_span: after a tenant has continuously and lawfully occupied a residential real property for 12 months, the owner of the residential real property shall not terminate a tenancy without just cause, which shall be stated in the written notice to terminate tenancy.

entries.explanation: Applies. Landlords generally cannot take more than one month's rent as a deposit (two for small landlords) and must return it with an itemized list within 21 days (Statewide rule: Cal. Civ. Code § 1950.5). No building-based coverage test applies.
entries.title: California security deposit cap and return rules
entries.requirement: A landlord may not demand or receive security exceeding one month's rent (two months' rent for small natural-person landlords owning no more than two properties with four units total, except when the tenant is a service member), and must return the deposit with an itemized statement within 21 calendar days after the tenant vacates. Security cannot be labeled nonrefundable, and bad-faith retention can bring statutory damages of up to twice the deposit.
entries.key_value: One month's rent cap (two months for small landlords); 21-day return deadline
entries.quoted_span: a landlord shall not demand or receive security, however denominated, in an amount or value in excess of an amount equal to one month’s rent, in addition to any rent for the first month paid on or before initial occupancy.

entries.explanation: Applies. Landlords can charge only actual screening costs, never over $30 (adjusted for inflation), and must give an itemized receipt (Statewide rule: Cal. Civ. Code § 1950.6). No building-based coverage test applies.
entries.title: California application screening fee limits
entries.requirement: A landlord may charge an application screening fee only up to actual out-of-pocket costs and the reasonable value of time spent, never more than $30 per applicant (adjustable annually with CPI since 1998), and may not charge it when no unit is or will soon be available. The landlord must either consider applications in order and approve the first qualified applicant (charging only when an application is actually considered), or refund the full fee within 7 days of selecting a tenant or 30 days of application, whichever is first; an itemized receipt is required.
entries.key_value: $30 per applicant, CPI-adjusted; itemized receipt required
entries.quoted_span: In no case shall the amount of the application screening fee charged by the landlord or their agent be greater than thirty dollars ($30) per applicant.

entries.explanation: Applies. Landlords cannot discriminate against applicants or tenants because of their income source, including housing vouchers (Statewide rule: California Fair Employment and Housing Act (FEHA); Cal. Gov. Code § 12955). No building-based coverage test applies.
entries.title: California FEHA housing screening limits
entries.citation: California Fair Employment and Housing Act (FEHA); Cal. Gov. Code § 12955
entries.requirement: Owners may not discriminate against or harass a person because of source of income (including Section 8 and HUD-VASH vouchers and other public assistance). Where a government rent subsidy applies, income standards must be based on the tenant's share of rent, and applicants must be allowed to offer alternative evidence of ability to pay instead of credit history; owners may still ask about the level or source of income.
entries.key_value: Source of income protected; subsidy-based income test uses tenant's portion of rent
entries.quoted_span: For the owner of any housing accommodation to discriminate against or harass any person because of the race, color, religion, sex, gender, gender identity, gender expression, sexual orientation, marital status, national origin, ancestry, familial status, source of income,

entries.explanation: Applies. It is illegal to use or sell shared pricing software built on competitors' data to coordinate prices or force others to follow its prices (Statewide rule: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 16729). No building-based coverage test applies.
entries.title: California common pricing algorithm ban
entries.requirement: It is unlawful to use or distribute a common pricing algorithm, meaning software or other technology used by two or more persons that uses competitor data to recommend, align, set or influence a price, as part of a conspiracy to restrain trade, or to coerce another person to adopt the algorithm's recommended price or term. The text is general and does not name rental housing.
entries.quoted_span: It shall be unlawful for a person to use or distribute a common pricing algorithm as part of a contract, combination in the form of a trust, or conspiracy to restrain trade or commerce in violation of this chapter.

In Los Angeles, landlords of units outside rent stabilization need a legal reason to evict and must pay relocation help for no-fault evictions (Los Angeles, CA rule: Los Angeles Just Cause for Eviction Ordinance (JCO)). Not covered by Los Angeles Rent Stabilization Ordinance (LAMC ch. XV, art. 1) (r-0021). Not checked from parcel data: the building is not a transient hotel; the building is not a licensed care facility; the building is not a fraternity or sorority house. Applies to tenancies where: tenant lived there six months or original lease expired.
entries.title: Los Angeles Just Cause for Eviction Ordinance
entries.citation: Los Angeles Just Cause for Eviction Ordinance (JCO)
entries.requirement: Landlords may not terminate a covered tenancy without just cause. At-fault reasons include nonpayment, uncured lease violations, nuisance, and illegal use. No-fault reasons, such as owner or family move-in, demolition, or removal from the rental market, generally require relocation assistance to the tenant. Landlords may not evict for unpaid rent unless the amount owed exceeds the Fair Market Rent for the unit's bedroom size, and all eviction notices must be filed with LAHD within three business days of service.
entries.key_value: Relocation assistance for no-fault evictions; no eviction for rent owed below Fair Market Rent
entries.quoted_span: It prohibits terminations of tenancies without just cause and requires relocation assistance for no-fault evictions.

entries.explanation: Applies. New Jersey has no statewide rent control, but towns may adopt their own, and rent increases need proper written notice and cannot be unconscionable (Statewide rule: N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.1 et seq.; N.J.S.A. 2A:42-84.5). No building-based coverage test applies.
entries.title: NJ no state rent control; municipalities may adopt rent control
entries.requirement: The State of New Jersey has no laws that establish, govern or control rents, but municipalities may pass rent control or rent leveling ordinances enforced by local boards. Landlords may raise rent only by proper lease termination and written notice, the increase must not be unconscionable, and it must comply with any municipal rent control ordinance. Newly constructed multiple dwellings are exempt from local rent control for 30 years after completion of construction.
entries.key_value: No state cap; local rent control permitted; new multiple dwellings exempt 30 years
entries.quoted_span:
The State of New Jersey has no laws that establish, govern or control rents. Municipalities 
may pass an ordinance establishing rent control or rent leveling.

entries.explanation: Applies. Landlords can evict or refuse to renew a lease only for specific legal reasons and with a court order, after giving the required written notice (Statewide rule: N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.1 to 61.12).  Parcel data: built 1910, at least 5 units. Exemptions ruled out by that data: Owner-occupied premises with two or fewer rental units. Not checked from parcel data: the building is not a hotel or motel; unit held in trust for developmentally disabled family member.
entries.title: NJ Anti-Eviction Act
entries.requirement: A residential landlord may remove a tenant or refuse to renew a lease only for a statutory good cause and through a court judgment for possession. Each cause except nonpayment requires a written Notice to Quit with a cause-specific period (3 days to 3 years), some causes need a prior Notice to Cease, and removal for substantial health and safety violations requires relocation assistance first.
entries.key_value: Good cause required; Notice to Quit periods from 3 days up to 3 years depending on cause; relocation assistance of 6 times monthly rent for illegal occupancy evictions
entries.quoted_span:
No residential landlord may evict or fail to renew a 
lease, whether it is a written or an oral lease without good cause.
not_checked: the building is not a hotel or motel
unit held in trust for developmentally disabled family member

entries.explanation: Applies. Landlords cannot collect a security deposit above one and a half months' rent, and yearly increases to the deposit are capped at 10% (Statewide rule: N.J.S.A. 46:8-21.2; N.J.S.A. 46:8-19; N.J.S.A. 46:8-21.1).  Parcel data: built 1910, at least 5 units. Exemptions ruled out by that data: Owner-occupied two- or three-family dwelling.
entries.title: NJ Security Deposit Law
entries.requirement: A landlord may not collect a security deposit of more than one and one-half times one month's rent, and any yearly increase in the deposit may not exceed 10% of the current deposit. Prepaid rent held as security, including last month's rent, counts toward the cap, and a pet deposit cannot push the total above the cap.
entries.key_value: 1.5 x monthly rent; annual increase max 10% of current deposit
entries.quoted_span:
The maximum-security deposit to be collected by the landlord cannot be more than 
one and one-half times one month’s rent ( N.J.S.A. 46:8-21.2 ).

entries.explanation: Applies. Landlords cannot charge more than $50 (adjusted for inflation) to apply for a rental, except in one- or two-family homes (Statewide rule: N.J.S.A. 46:8-18.1).  Parcel data: built 1910, at least 5 units. Exemptions ruled out by that data: One- or two-family dwelling. Not checked from parcel data: real estate licensee who is not the landlord (depends on the tenancy).
entries.title: NJ rental application fee cap
entries.requirement: A landlord or agent may not require an application or similar fee to apply to lease or sublease a residential rental property that exceeds $50, adjusted annually for CPI increases. Violators face penalties of up to $500 (first), $750 (second) and $1,000 (subsequent offenses), and the amount wrongfully charged is remitted to the applicant.
entries.key_value: $50 cap (CPI-adjusted annually)
entries.quoted_span:
A landlord, or
agent thereof, shall not require an application or other similar fee to apply
to lease or sublease a residential rental property for dwelling purposes, which
exceeds $50.
not_checked: real estate licensee who is not the landlord (depends on the tenancy)

entries.explanation: Applies. Landlords cannot ask about or use an applicant's criminal record until after a conditional offer, and then only limited convictions with an individual review (Statewide rule: N.J.S.A. 46:8-52 et seq.).  Parcel data: built 1910, at least 5 units. Exemptions ruled out by that data: Owner-occupied premises of not more than four units.
entries.title: NJ Fair Chance in Housing Act
entries.requirement: Housing providers may not ask about or consider an applicant's criminal record before making a conditional offer. After a conditional offer, only certain convictions within set look-back periods may be considered, subject to an individualized assessment, written notice of withdrawal, and an appeal opportunity. Providers also may not require drug or alcohol tests of applicants.
entries.key_value: No criminal-record inquiry before conditional offer; look-back 6 years (1st degree), 4 years (2nd/3rd degree), 1 year (4th degree); serious listed offenses and lifetime sex-offender registration have no look-back limit
entries.quoted_span:
A housing
provider
shall not make any oral or written inquiry
regarding an applicant’s criminal record prior to making a conditional offer.

entries.explanation: Applies. Landlords cannot refuse to rent because of an applicant's lawful income source, but may still turn down applicants for too little income or bad credit (Statewide rule: N.J.S.A. 10:5-12; New Jersey Law Against Discrimination (N.J.S.A. 10:5-1 et seq.)).  Parcel data: built 1910, at least 5 units. Exemptions ruled out by that data: Two-family owner-occupied dwelling; Room in owner- or resident-occupied single home.
entries.title: NJ Law Against Discrimination source-of-income ban
entries.citation: N.J.S.A. 10:5-12; New Jersey Law Against Discrimination (N.J.S.A. 10:5-1 et seq.)
entries.requirement: The New Jersey Law Against Discrimination requires equal treatment in renting housing regardless of listed characteristics, including source of lawful income. A landlord may still refuse to rent for insufficient income or poor credit history.
entries.key_value: Source of lawful income is a protected class
entries.quoted_span:
prohibits discrimination when selling or renting property and requires 
equal treatment in the sale or rental of housing regardless of race, creed, color, national origin,

entries.explanation: Not yet effective. Rental owners and software coordinators cannot use algorithms that pool competitors' data to coordinate rent prices, and breaking this counts as an antitrust violation (Statewide rule: P.L. 2026, c.43 (C.56:9-20 to 56:9-26)). It takes effect 2027-07-01; the as-of date is 2026-10-01. Flagged: possible conflict with Jersey City Code § 218-12 (r-0043); needs human review.
entries.title: NJ FAIR Act algorithmic rent-setting ban
entries.requirement: It is unlawful for rental property owners to pay for or use a coordinator's services, for coordinators to perform a coordinating function or facilitate agreements restricting competition, and for any persons to engage in or facilitate parallel pricing coordination through algorithmic pricing. Violations are treated as violations of the New Jersey Antitrust Act, and municipalities may not enact conflicting ordinances.
entries.key_value: Bans use or operation of algorithmic rent-setting that pools competitively sensitive information or sets parallel prices
entries.conflict_note: Possible conflict with Jersey City Code § 218-12 (r-0043); needs human review. Possible conflict with Hoboken City Code § 158-2 (Ord. No. B-781) (r-0046); needs human review.

entries.explanation: Applies. Jersey City regulates rent increases in buildings with five or more units; buildings with one to four units are exempt (Jersey City, NJ rule: Jersey City Municipal Code ch. 260). 5 or more units (New Jersey property class 4C (apartments, 5 or more units)): meets the test (units >= 5).
entries.title: Jersey City Rent Control Ordinance
entries.requirement: The city administers and enforces a rent control ordinance that regulates rent increases, with landlord applications for capital improvement, vacancy and hardship increases and tenant petitions for illegal rent. Properties with 1-4 units are exempt from rent control.
entries.quoted_span:
The Office of Landlord Tenant Relations administers and enforces the
Rent Control Ordinance, Chapter 260
of the Jersey City Municipal Code

entries.explanation: Applies. Jersey City bans landlords from using algorithmic rent coordination services, with fines up to $2,000 per day (Jersey City, NJ rule: Jersey City Code § 218-12). entries.requirement: Jersey City prohibits a landlord's use of algorithmic rent coordination services, with public and private enforcement and fines up to $2,000 per day.

entries.citation: Los Angeles Rent Stabilization Ordinance (LAMC ch. XV, art. 1)
entries.requirement: Landlords of RSO units may raise rent only once every 12 months by the allowable percentage published by LAHD. Rent may be reset to market only in listed circumstances, such as the tenant voluntarily moving out or being evicted for cause.

entries.quoted_span: Rent may be increased once every 12 months by the allowable rent increase percentage

entries.explanation: Applies. The State of New Jersey has no laws that establish, govern or control rents. Municipalities 
may pass an ordinance establishing rent control or rent leveling.

entries.explanation: Applies. Landlords can evict or refuse to renew a lease only for specific legal reasons and with a court order, after giving the required written notice (Statewide rule: N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.1 to 61.12).  Parcel data: built 1912, at least 5 units. Exemptions ruled out by that data: Owner-occupied premises with two or fewer rental units. Not checked from parcel data: the building is not a hotel or motel; unit held in trust for developmentally disabled family member.
entries.title: NJ Anti-Eviction Act
entries.requirement: A residential landlord may remove a tenant or refuse to renew a lease only for a statutory good cause and through a court judgment for possession. Each cause except nonpayment requires a written Notice to Quit with a cause-specific period (3 days to 3 years), some causes need a prior Notice to Cease, and removal for substantial health and safety violations requires relocation assistance first.
entries.key_value: Good cause required; Notice to Quit periods from 3 days up to 3 years depending on cause; relocation assistance of 6 times monthly rent for illegal occupancy evictions
entries.quoted_span:
No residential landlord may evict or fail to renew a 
lease, whether it is a written or an oral lease without good cause.
not_checked: the building is not a hotel or motel
unit held in trust for developmentally disabled family member

entries.explanation: Applies. Landlords cannot collect a security deposit above one and a half months' rent, and yearly increases to the deposit are capped at 10% (Statewide rule: N.J.S.A. 46:8-21.2; N.J.S.A. 46:8-19; N.J.S.A. 46:8-21.1).  Parcel data: built 1912, at least 5 units. Exemptions ruled out by that data: Owner-occupied two- or three-family dwelling.
entries.title: NJ Security Deposit Law
entries.requirement: A landlord may not collect a security deposit of more than one and one-half times one month's rent, and any yearly increase in the deposit may not exceed 10% of the current deposit. Prepaid rent held as security, including last month's rent, counts toward the cap, and a pet deposit cannot push the total above the cap.
entries.key_value: 1.5 x monthly rent; annual increase max 10% of current deposit
entries.quoted_span:
The maximum-security deposit to be collected by the landlord cannot be more than 
one and one-half times one month’s rent ( N.J.S.A. 46:8-21.2 ).

entries.explanation: Applies. Landlords cannot charge more than $50 (adjusted for inflation) to apply for a rental, except in one- or two-family homes (Statewide rule: N.J.S.A. 46:8-18.1).  Parcel data: built 1912, at least 5 units. Exemptions ruled out by that data: One- or two-family dwelling. Not checked from parcel data: real estate licensee who is not the landlord (depends on the tenancy).
entries.title: NJ rental application fee cap
entries.requirement: A landlord or agent may not require an application or similar fee to apply to lease or sublease a residential rental property that exceeds $50, adjusted annually for CPI increases. Violators face penalties of up to $500 (first), $750 (second) and $1,000 (subsequent offenses), and the amount wrongfully charged is remitted to the applicant.
entries.key_value: $50 cap (CPI-adjusted annually)
entries.quoted_span:
A landlord, or
agent thereof, shall not require an application or other similar fee to apply
to lease or sublease a residential rental property for dwelling purposes, which
exceeds $50.
not_checked: real estate licensee who is not the landlord (depends on the tenancy)

entries.explanation: Applies. Landlords cannot ask about or use an applicant's criminal record until after a conditional offer, and then only limited convictions with an individual review (Statewide rule: N.J.S.A. 46:8-52 et seq.).  Parcel data: built 1912, at least 5 units. Exemptions ruled out by that data: Owner-occupied premises of not more than four units.
entries.title: NJ Fair Chance in Housing Act
entries.requirement: Housing providers may not ask about or consider an applicant's criminal record before making a conditional offer. After a conditional offer, only certain convictions within set look-back periods may be considered, subject to an individualized assessment, written notice of withdrawal, and an appeal opportunity. Providers also may not require drug or alcohol tests of applicants.
entries.key_value: No criminal-record inquiry before conditional offer; look-back 6 years (1st degree), 4 years (2nd/3rd degree), 1 year (4th degree); serious listed offenses and lifetime sex-offender registration have no look-back limit
entries.quoted_span:
A housing
provider
shall not make any oral or written inquiry
regarding an applicant’s criminal record prior to making a conditional offer.

entries.explanation: Applies. Landlords cannot refuse to rent because of an applicant's lawful income source, but may still turn down applicants for too little income or bad credit (Statewide rule: N.J.S.A. 10:5-12; New Jersey Law Against Discrimination (N.J.S.A. 10:5-1 et seq.)).  Parcel data: built 1912, at least 5 units. Exemptions ruled out by that data: Two-family owner-occupied dwelling; Room in owner- or resident-occupied single home.
entries.title: NJ Law Against Discrimination source-of-income ban
entries.citation: N.J.S.A. 10:5-12; New Jersey Law Against Discrimination (N.J.S.A. 10:5-1 et seq.)
entries.requirement: The New Jersey Law Against Discrimination requires equal treatment in renting housing regardless of listed characteristics, including source of lawful income. A landlord may still refuse to rent for insufficient income or poor credit history.
entries.key_value: Source of lawful income is a protected class
entries.quoted_span:
prohibits discrimination when selling or renting property and requires 
equal treatment in the sale or rental of housing regardless of race, creed, color, national origin,

entries.explanation: Not yet effective. Rental owners and software coordinators cannot use algorithms that pool competitors' data to coordinate rent prices, and breaking this counts as an antitrust violation (Statewide rule: P.L. 2026, c.43 (C.56:9-20 to 56:9-26)). It takes effect 2027-07-01; the as-of date is 2026-10-01. Flagged: possible conflict with Jersey City Code § 218-12 (r-0043); needs human review.
entries.title: NJ FAIR Act algorithmic rent-setting ban
entries.requirement: It is unlawful for rental property owners to pay for or use a coordinator's services, for coordinators to perform a coordinating function or facilitate agreements restricting competition, and for any persons to engage in or facilitate parallel pricing coordination through algorithmic pricing. Violations are treated as violations of the New Jersey Antitrust Act, and municipalities may not enact conflicting ordinances.
entries.key_value: Bans use or operation of algorithmic rent-setting that pools competitively sensitive information or sets parallel prices
entries.conflict_note: Possible conflict with Jersey City Code § 218-12 (r-0043); needs human review. Possible conflict with Hoboken City Code § 158-2 (Ord. No. B-781) (r-0046); needs human review.

entries.title: Jersey City Rent Control Ordinance
entries.requirement: The city administers and enforces a rent control ordinance that regulates rent increases, with landlord applications for capital improvement, vacancy and hardship increases and tenant petitions for illegal rent. Properties with 1-4 units are exempt from rent control.
entries.quoted_span:
The Office of Landlord Tenant Relations administers and enforces the
Rent Control Ordinance, Chapter 260
of the Jersey City Municipal Code

entries.explanation: Applies. Landlords generally cannot take more than one month's rent as a deposit (two for small landlords) and must return it with an itemized list within 21 days (Statewide rule: Cal. Civ. Code § 1950.5). No building-based coverage test applies.
entries.title: California security deposit cap and return rules
entries.requirement: A landlord may not demand or receive security exceeding one month's rent (two months' rent for small natural-person landlords owning no more than two properties with four units total, except when the tenant is a service member), and must return the deposit with an itemized statement within 21 calendar days after the tenant vacates. Security cannot be labeled nonrefundable, and bad-faith retention can bring statutory damages of up to twice the deposit.
entries.key_value: One month's rent cap (two months for small landlords); 21-day return deadline
entries.quoted_span: a landlord shall not demand or receive security, however denominated, in an amount or value in excess of an amount equal to one month’s rent, in addition to any rent for the first month paid on or before initial occupancy.

entries.explanation: Applies. Landlords can charge only actual screening costs, never over $30 (adjusted for inflation), and must give an itemized receipt (Statewide rule: Cal. Civ. Code § 1950.6). No building-based coverage test applies.
entries.title: California application screening fee limits
entries.requirement: A landlord may charge an application screening fee only up to actual out-of-pocket costs and the reasonable value of time spent, never more than $30 per applicant (adjustable annually with CPI since 1998), and may not charge it when no unit is or will soon be available. The landlord must either consider applications in order and approve the first qualified applicant (charging only when an application is actually considered), or refund the full fee within 7 days of selecting a tenant or 30 days of application, whichever is first; an itemized receipt is required.
entries.key_value: $30 per applicant, CPI-adjusted; itemized receipt required
entries.quoted_span: In no case shall the amount of the application screening fee charged by the landlord or their agent be greater than thirty dollars ($30) per applicant.

entries.title: California FEHA housing screening limits
entries.citation: California Fair Employment and Housing Act (FEHA); Cal. Gov. Code § 12955
entries.requirement: Owners may not discriminate against or harass a person because of source of income (including Section 8 and HUD-VASH vouchers and other public assistance). entries.title: California common pricing algorithm ban
entries.requirement: It is unlawful to use or distribute a common pricing algorithm, meaning software or other technology used by two or more persons that uses competitor data to recommend, align, set or influence a price, as part of a conspiracy to restrain trade, or to coerce another person to adopt the algorithm's recommended price or term. entries.quoted_span: It shall be unlawful for a person to use or distribute a common pricing algorithm as part of a contract, combination in the form of a trust, or conspiracy to restrain trade or commerce in violation of this chapter.

entries.explanation: Applies. Landlords generally cannot take more than one month's rent as a deposit (two for small landlords) and must return it with an itemized list within 21 days (Statewide rule: Cal. Civ. Code § 1950.5). No building-based coverage test applies.
entries.title: California security deposit cap and return rules
entries.requirement: A landlord may not demand or receive security exceeding one month's rent (two months' rent for small natural-person landlords owning no more than two properties with four units total, except when the tenant is a service member), and must return the deposit with an itemized statement within 21 calendar days after the tenant vacates. entries.explanation: Applies. Landlords can charge only actual screening costs, never over $30 (adjusted for inflation), and must give an itemized receipt (Statewide rule: Cal. Civ. Code § 1950.6). No building-based coverage test applies.
entries.title: California application screening fee limits
entries.requirement: A landlord may charge an application screening fee only up to actual out-of-pocket costs and the reasonable value of time spent, never more than $30 per applicant (adjustable annually with CPI since 1998), and may not charge it when no unit is or will soon be available. entries.quoted_span: In no case shall the amount of the application screening fee charged by the landlord or their agent be greater than thirty dollars ($30) per applicant.

entries.explanation: Applies. Landlords generally cannot take more than one month's rent as a deposit (two for small landlords) and must return it with an itemized list within 21 days (Statewide rule: Cal. Civ. Code § 1950.5). No building-based coverage test applies.
entries.title: California security deposit cap and return rules
entries.requirement: A landlord may not demand or receive security exceeding one month's rent (two months' rent for small natural-person landlords owning no more than two properties with four units total, except when the tenant is a service member), and must return the deposit with an itemized statement within 21 calendar days after the tenant vacates. entries.explanation: Applies. Landlords can charge only actual screening costs, never over $30 (adjusted for inflation), and must give an itemized receipt (Statewide rule: Cal. Civ. Code § 1950.6). No building-based coverage test applies.
entries.title: California application screening fee limits
entries.requirement: A landlord may charge an application screening fee only up to actual out-of-pocket costs and the reasonable value of time spent, never more than $30 per applicant (adjustable annually with CPI since 1998), and may not charge it when no unit is or will soon be available. entries.key_value: $30 per applicant, CPI-adjusted; itemized receipt required
entries.quoted_span: In no case shall the amount of the application screening fee charged by the landlord or their agent be greater than thirty dollars ($30) per applicant.

entries.explanation: Applies. New Jersey has no statewide rent control, but towns may adopt their own, and rent increases need proper written notice and cannot be unconscionable (Statewide rule: N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.1 et seq.; N.J.S.A. 2A:42-84.5). No building-based coverage test applies.
entries.title: NJ no state rent control; municipalities may adopt rent control
entries.requirement: The State of New Jersey has no laws that establish, govern or control rents, but municipalities may pass rent control or rent leveling ordinances enforced by local boards. Landlords may raise rent only by proper lease termination and written notice, the increase must not be unconscionable, and it must comply with any municipal rent control ordinance. Newly constructed multiple dwellings are exempt from local rent control for 30 years after completion of construction.
entries.key_value: No state cap; local rent control permitted; new multiple dwellings exempt 30 years
entries.quoted_span:
The State of New Jersey has no laws that establish, govern or control rents. Municipalities 
may pass an ordinance establishing rent control or rent leveling.

entries.explanation: Applies. Landlords can evict or refuse to renew a lease only for specific legal reasons and with a court order, after giving the required written notice (Statewide rule: N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.1 to 61.12).  Parcel data: at least 5 units. Exemptions ruled out by that data: Owner-occupied premises with two or fewer rental units. Not checked from parcel data: the building is not a hotel or motel; unit held in trust for developmentally disabled family member.
entries.title: NJ Anti-Eviction Act
entries.requirement: A residential landlord may remove a tenant or refuse to renew a lease only for a statutory good cause and through a court judgment for possession. Each cause except nonpayment requires a written Notice to Quit with a cause-specific period (3 days to 3 years), some causes need a prior Notice to Cease, and removal for substantial health and safety violations requires relocation assistance first.
entries.key_value: Good cause required; Notice to Quit periods from 3 days up to 3 years depending on cause; relocation assistance of 6 times monthly rent for illegal occupancy evictions
entries.quoted_span:
No residential landlord may evict or fail to renew a 
lease, whether it is a written or an oral lease without good cause.
not_checked: the building is not a hotel or motel
unit held in trust for developmentally disabled family member

entries.explanation: Applies. Landlords cannot collect a security deposit above one and a half months' rent, and yearly increases to the deposit are capped at 10% (Statewide rule: N.J.S.A. 46:8-21.2; N.J.S.A. 46:8-19; N.J.S.A. 46:8-21.1).  Parcel data: at least 5 units. Exemptions ruled out by that data: Owner-occupied two- or three-family dwelling.
entries.title: NJ Security Deposit Law
entries.requirement: A landlord may not collect a security deposit of more than one and one-half times one month's rent, and any yearly increase in the deposit may not exceed 10% of the current deposit. Prepaid rent held as security, including last month's rent, counts toward the cap, and a pet deposit cannot push the total above the cap.
entries.key_value: 1.5 x monthly rent; annual increase max 10% of current deposit
entries.quoted_span:
The maximum-security deposit to be collected by the landlord cannot be more than 
one and one-half times one month’s rent ( N.J.S.A. 46:8-21.2 ).

entries.explanation: Applies. Landlords cannot charge more than $50 (adjusted for inflation) to apply for a rental, except in one- or two-family homes (Statewide rule: N.J.S.A. 46:8-18.1).  Parcel data: at least 5 units. Exemptions ruled out by that data: One- or two-family dwelling. Not checked from parcel data: real estate licensee who is not the landlord (depends on the tenancy).
entries.title: NJ rental application fee cap
entries.requirement: A landlord or agent may not require an application or similar fee to apply to lease or sublease a residential rental property that exceeds $50, adjusted annually for CPI increases. Violators face penalties of up to $500 (first), $750 (second) and $1,000 (subsequent offenses), and the amount wrongfully charged is remitted to the applicant.
entries.key_value: $50 cap (CPI-adjusted annually)
entries.quoted_span:
A landlord, or
agent thereof, shall not require an application or other similar fee to apply
to lease or sublease a residential rental property for dwelling purposes, which
exceeds $50.
not_checked: real estate licensee who is not the landlord (depends on the tenancy)

entries.explanation: Applies. Landlords cannot ask about or use an applicant's criminal record until after a conditional offer, and then only limited convictions with an individual review (Statewide rule: N.J.S.A. 46:8-52 et seq.).  Parcel data: at least 5 units. Exemptions ruled out by that data: Owner-occupied premises of not more than four units.
entries.title: NJ Fair Chance in Housing Act
entries.requirement: Housing providers may not ask about or consider an applicant's criminal record before making a conditional offer. After a conditional offer, only certain convictions within set look-back periods may be considered, subject to an individualized assessment, written notice of withdrawal, and an appeal opportunity. Providers also may not require drug or alcohol tests of applicants.
entries.key_value: No criminal-record inquiry before conditional offer; look-back 6 years (1st degree), 4 years (2nd/3rd degree), 1 year (4th degree); serious listed offenses and lifetime sex-offender registration have no look-back limit
entries.quoted_span:
A housing
provider
shall not make any oral or written inquiry
regarding an applicant’s criminal record prior to making a conditional offer.

entries.explanation: Applies. Landlords cannot refuse to rent because of an applicant's lawful income source, but may still turn down applicants for too little income or bad credit (Statewide rule: N.J.S.A. 10:5-12; New Jersey Law Against Discrimination (N.J.S.A. 10:5-1 et seq.)).  Parcel data: at least 5 units. Exemptions ruled out by that data: Two-family owner-occupied dwelling; Room in owner- or resident-occupied single home.
entries.title: NJ Law Against Discrimination source-of-income ban
entries.citation: N.J.S.A. 10:5-12; New Jersey Law Against Discrimination (N.J.S.A. 10:5-1 et seq.)
entries.requirement: The New Jersey Law Against Discrimination requires equal treatment in renting housing regardless of listed characteristics, including source of lawful income. A landlord may still refuse to rent for insufficient income or poor credit history.

entries.quoted_span:
prohibits discrimination when selling or renting property and requires 
equal treatment in the sale or rental of housing regardless of race, creed, color, national origin,

It takes effect 2027-07-01; the as-of date is 2026-10-01.
entries.title: NJ FAIR Act algorithmic rent-setting ban
entries.requirement: It is unlawful for rental property owners to pay for or use a coordinator's services, for coordinators to perform a coordinating function or facilitate agreements restricting competition, and for any persons to engage in or facilitate parallel pricing coordination through algorithmic pricing. Violations are treated as violations of the New Jersey Antitrust Act, and municipalities may not enact conflicting ordinances.

entries.title: Newark Rent Control Ordinance

Increases are barred if the dwelling is not in substantial compliance or the landlord has not registered, and require 30 days' written notice to the tenant and the Rent Regulation Officer.

In no case shall the allowable rent increase exceed 4%.
