entries.explanation: Applies. Landlords generally cannot take more than one month's rent as a deposit (two for small landlords) and must return it with an itemized list within 21 days (Statewide rule: Cal. Civ. Code § 1950.5). No building-based coverage test applies.
entries.title: California security deposit cap and return rules
entries.requirement: A landlord may not demand or receive security exceeding one month's rent (two months' rent for small natural-person landlords owning no more than two properties with four units total, except when the tenant is a service member), and must return the deposit with an itemized statement within 21 calendar days after the tenant vacates. Security cannot be labeled nonrefundable, and bad-faith retention can bring statutory damages of up to twice the deposit.
entries.key_value: One month's rent cap (two months for small landlords); 21-day return deadline
entries.quoted_span: a landlord shall not demand or receive security, however denominated, in an amount or value in excess of an amount equal to one month’s rent, in addition to any rent for the first month paid on or before initial occupancy.

entries.explanation: Applies. Landlords can charge only actual screening costs, never over $30 (adjusted for inflation), and must give an itemized receipt (Statewide rule: Cal. Civ. Code § 1950.6). No building-based coverage test applies.
entries.title: California application screening fee limits
entries.requirement: A landlord may charge an application screening fee only up to actual out-of-pocket costs and the reasonable value of time spent, never more than $30 per applicant (adjustable annually with CPI since 1998), and may not charge it when no unit is or will soon be available. The landlord must either consider applications in order and approve the first qualified applicant (charging only when an application is actually considered), or refund the full fee within 7 days of selecting a tenant or 30 days of application, whichever is first; an itemized receipt is required.
entries.key_value: $30 per applicant, CPI-adjusted; itemized receipt required
entries.quoted_span: In no case shall the amount of the application screening fee charged by the landlord or their agent be greater than thirty dollars ($30) per applicant.

entries.explanation: Applies. Landlords cannot discriminate against applicants or tenants because of their income source, including housing vouchers (Statewide rule: California Fair Employment and Housing Act (FEHA); Cal. Gov. Code § 12955). No building-based coverage test applies.
entries.title: California FEHA housing screening limits
entries.citation: California Fair Employment and Housing Act (FEHA); Cal. Gov. Code § 12955
entries.requirement: Owners may not discriminate against or harass a person because of source of income (including Section 8 and HUD-VASH vouchers and other public assistance). Where a government rent subsidy applies, income standards must be based on the tenant's share of rent, and applicants must be allowed to offer alternative evidence of ability to pay instead of credit history; owners may still ask about the level or source of income.
entries.key_value: Source of income protected; subsidy-based income test uses tenant's portion of rent
entries.quoted_span: For the owner of any housing accommodation to discriminate against or harass any person because of the race, color, religion, sex, gender, gender identity, gender expression, sexual orientation, marital status, national origin, ancestry, familial status, source of income,

entries.explanation: Applies. It is illegal to use or sell shared pricing software built on competitors' data to coordinate prices or force others to follow its prices (Statewide rule: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 16729). No building-based coverage test applies.
entries.title: California common pricing algorithm ban
entries.requirement: It is unlawful to use or distribute a common pricing algorithm, meaning software or other technology used by two or more persons that uses competitor data to recommend, align, set or influence a price, as part of a conspiracy to restrain trade, or to coerce another person to adopt the algorithm's recommended price or term. The text is general and does not name rental housing.
entries.quoted_span: It shall be unlawful for a person to use or distribute a common pricing algorithm as part of a contract, combination in the form of a trust, or conspiracy to restrain trade or commerce in violation of this chapter.

entries.title: San Francisco annual allowable rent increase
entries.requirement: For rent-controlled units, the annual allowable rent increase effective March 1, 2026 through February 28, 2027 is 1.6% of the tenant's base rent.
entries.key_value: 1.6% annual allowable increase
entries.quoted_span: For rent-controlled units, the annual allowable increase amount effective March 1, 2026 through February 28, 2027 is 1.6%.

entries.explanation: Applies. San Francisco landlords can evict tenants in covered units only for one of 17 listed reasons, and ending a lease or selling the building is not enough (San Francisco, CA rule: S.F. Admin. Code ch. 37). No building-based coverage test applies.
entries.title: San Francisco Rent Ordinance just cause and relocation
entries.requirement: A landlord may evict a tenant from a unit covered by the Rent Ordinance only for one of 17 listed just cause reasons, which must be the dominant motive for the eviction. Expiration of a rental agreement or a change in ownership is not just cause.
entries.key_value: 17 just cause reasons (Ordinance § 37.9(a))
entries.quoted_span: In order to evict a tenant from a rental unit covered by the Rent Ordinance, a landlord must have a "just cause" reason that is the dominant motive for pursuing the eviction.

entries.explanation: Applies. Landlords can ask for no more than first and last month's rent, a one-month deposit and a key and lock cost, and must return the deposit within 30 days (Statewide rule: G.L. c. 186 § 15B). entries.title: Massachusetts security deposit law

The deposit must be held in a separate interest-bearing Massachusetts bank account, accrue 5% annual interest (or the lesser bank rate) after one year, and be returned with itemized deductions within 30 days after the tenancy ends.

entries.explanation: Applies. A rental broker can work for the tenant or the landlord but not both, and only the party who hired the broker pays the fee (Statewide rule: G.L. c. 112 § 87DDD1/2). No building-based coverage test applies.
entries.title: Massachusetts broker fee rule
entries.requirement: A licensed broker or salesperson may contract solely with the prospective tenant or solely with the landlord, not both. Any broker fee may only be paid by the party (lessor or tenant) who originally engaged and contracted with the broker.
entries.key_value: Fee paid only by the party who hired the broker
entries.quoted_span: Any fee shall only be paid by the party, lessor or tenant who originally engaged and entered into a contract with the licensed broker or salesperson.

entries.explanation: Applies. New Jersey has no statewide rent control, but towns may adopt their own, and rent increases need proper written notice and cannot be unconscionable (Statewide rule: N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.1 et seq.; N.J.S.A. 2A:42-84.5). No building-based coverage test applies.
entries.title: NJ no state rent control; municipalities may adopt rent control
entries.requirement: The State of New Jersey has no laws that establish, govern or control rents, but municipalities may pass rent control or rent leveling ordinances enforced by local boards. Landlords may raise rent only by proper lease termination and written notice, the increase must not be unconscionable, and it must comply with any municipal rent control ordinance. Newly constructed multiple dwellings are exempt from local rent control for 30 years after completion of construction.
entries.key_value: No state cap; local rent control permitted; new multiple dwellings exempt 30 years
entries.quoted_span:
The State of New Jersey has no laws that establish, govern or control rents. Municipalities 
may pass an ordinance establishing rent control or rent leveling.

entries.explanation: Applies. entries.title: NJ Anti-Eviction Act
entries.requirement: A residential landlord may remove a tenant or refuse to renew a lease only for a statutory good cause and through a court judgment for possession. Each cause except nonpayment requires a written Notice to Quit with a cause-specific period (3 days to 3 years), some causes need a prior Notice to Cease, and removal for substantial health and safety violations requires relocation assistance first.
entries.key_value: Good cause required; Notice to Quit periods from 3 days up to 3 years depending on cause; relocation assistance of 6 times monthly rent for illegal occupancy evictions

No residential landlord may evict or fail to renew a 
lease, whether it is a written or an oral lease without good cause.

entries.explanation: Applies. entries.title: NJ Security Deposit Law
entries.requirement: A landlord may not collect a security deposit of more than one and one-half times one month's rent, and any yearly increase in the deposit may not exceed 10% of the current deposit. Prepaid rent held as security, including last month's rent, counts toward the cap, and a pet deposit cannot push the total above the cap.

entries.explanation: Applies. A rental broker can work for the tenant or the landlord but not both, and only the party who hired the broker pays the fee (Statewide rule: G.L. c. 112 § 87DDD1/2). No building-based coverage test applies.

entries.explanation: Applies. Landlords generally cannot take more than one month's rent as a deposit (two for small landlords) and must return it with an itemized list within 21 days (Statewide rule: Cal. Civ. Code § 1950.5). No building-based coverage test applies.

entries.explanation: Applies. New Jersey has no statewide rent control, but towns may adopt their own, and rent increases need proper written notice and cannot be unconscionable (Statewide rule: N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.1 et seq.; N.J.S.A. 2A:42-84.5). No building-based coverage test applies.
entries.title: NJ no state rent control; municipalities may adopt rent control
entries.requirement: The State of New Jersey has no laws that establish, govern or control rents, but municipalities may pass rent control or rent leveling ordinances enforced by local boards. Landlords may raise rent only by proper lease termination and written notice, the increase must not be unconscionable, and it must comply with any municipal rent control ordinance. Newly constructed multiple dwellings are exempt from local rent control for 30 years after completion of construction.
entries.key_value: No state cap; local rent control permitted; new multiple dwellings exempt 30 years
entries.quoted_span:
The State of New Jersey has no laws that establish, govern or control rents. Municipalities 
may pass an ordinance establishing rent control or rent leveling.

No building-based coverage test applies. Applies to tenancies where: evicted for owner move-in or Ellis Act withdrawal.
entries.title: Berkeley relocation assistance for owner move-in and Ellis Act evictions
entries.citation: Berkeley Rent Stabilization and Good Cause for Eviction Ordinance; Berkeley Ellis Implementation Ordinance
entries.requirement: Owners must pay tenants relocation assistance when evicting for an owner move-in or to withdraw a unit from the rental market under the Ellis Act. The payment amounts are indexed to inflation and adjusted each year by the Rent Board.
entries.key_value: Standard payment $19,413; additional payment for qualifying households $6,471 (effective 2026-01-01; 1.5% CPI adjustment)
entries.quoted_span: The Rent Stabilization and Good Cause for Eviction Ordinance requires owners to pay tenants relocation assistance in the event of an owner move-in eviction.

entries.explanation: Unknown. Berkeley tenants in covered units can be evicted only for just cause, and owners cannot evict over small rental debts or for refusing a new fixed-term lease (Berkeley, CA rule: Berkeley Rent Stabilization Ordinance (as amended by Measure BB)). Coverage depends on: year built is missing in the parcel data (needed: first occupied before 1980-01-01).
entries.title: Berkeley just cause for eviction
entries.citation: Berkeley Rent Stabilization Ordinance (as amended by Measure BB)
entries.requirement: Tenants in fully or partially covered units cannot be evicted without just cause. Measure BB bars eviction for rental debt under one month of Fair Market Rent or for refusing to sign a new fixed-term lease, requires lease-breach evictions to show substantial actual harm and unreasonable tenant behavior, and requires notices to be filed with the Rent Board within three business days.
entries.key_value: Nonpayment eviction only if debt >= one month's Fair Market Rent
entries.quoted_span: In Berkeley, tenants in units that are fully or partially covered by the Rent Ordinance cannot be evicted unless there is "just cause” (previously called “good cause”).

entries.explanation: Unknown. Berkeley landlords of covered units must pay tenants interest on security deposits each year, prorated if the tenant moves out early (Berkeley, CA rule: Berkeley Rent Stabilization Ordinance). Coverage depends on: requires fully or partially covered by Berkeley Rent Ordinance, which is not in the parcel data.
entries.title: Berkeley security deposit interest requirement
entries.requirement: For tenancies in units fully or partially covered by the Berkeley Rent Ordinance, landlords must pay tenants interest on the security deposit at the end of each year, and a prorated amount if the tenant moves out before year end.
entries.key_value: Annual interest on deposit, prorated on move-out
entries.quoted_span: landlords must pay tenants interest on their security deposit at the end of each year and a prorated amount if the tenant moves out before the end of the year.

entries.explanation: Applies. Berkeley landlords must disclose tenant screening fee rights and the state fee cap, and cannot charge non-refundable renewal or roommate-change fees (Berkeley, CA rule: Berkeley Municipal Code ch. 13.78). No building-based coverage test applies.
entries.title: Berkeley screening fee disclosure ordinance
entries.requirement: Owners charging a fee for a credit report or application processing must provide a clear tenant screening fee rights statement and the state maximum fee cap before receiving the fee. Owners may not charge existing tenants a non-refundable fee for renewing a tenancy or for adding, replacing, or removing a roommate.
entries.key_value: Disclosure of Cal. Civ. Code 1950.6(b) fee cap; no non-refundable renewal or roommate fees
entries.quoted_span: An owner of residential rental property (or the owner’s agent) cannot charge a non-refundable fee to any existing tenant for the purpose of renewing a tenancy, in whole or in part,

entries.explanation: Applies. Berkeley landlords cannot ask about or use criminal history in choosing or managing tenants, and must give written notice and a chance to respond first (Berkeley, CA rule: Berkeley Municipal Code ch. 13.106).  Parcel data: at least 5 units. Exemptions ruled out by that data: Owner-occupied 1-3 unit property. Not checked from parcel data: lifetime sex offender (depends on the tenancy); public housing or Section 8 property; owner move-back rental agreement (depends on the tenancy).
entries.title: Berkeley Fair Chance Access to Housing Ordinance
entries.requirement: Rental housing providers may not ask about or use criminal history in advertising, applications, tenant selection, or tenancy decisions, and must give written notice and an opportunity to respond before taking any action based on criminal history. Violations carry administrative fines of $1,000 to $10,000 per violation plus civil damages.
entries.key_value: Criminal history inquiries and use prohibited; fines $1,000-$10,000 per violation
entries.quoted_span: The Fair Chance Access to Housing Ordinance prohibits rental housing providers in Berkeley from asking about and using criminal history and/or criminal background checks in their rental housing advertising, applications, tenant selection process, or decision-making.

entries.explanation: Applies. In Berkeley, landlords cannot use pricing software that relies on competitors' private data to set rents, with fines up to $1,000 per violation (Berkeley, CA rule: Berkeley Municipal Code ch. 13.63). No building-based coverage test applies.
entries.title: Berkeley ban on coordinated rent-pricing algorithms
entries.requirement: It is unlawful to sell, license, or provide to Berkeley landlords, or for a landlord to use, a coordinated pricing algorithm that uses non-public competitor data to set or recommend rents or occupancy levels for residential units. Each month and each unit constitutes a separate violation, with civil penalties up to $1,000 per violation plus attorney's fees.
entries.key_value: Ban on coordinated pricing algorithms; civil penalties up to $1,000 per violation
entries.quoted_span:
It shall be unlawful for a landlord to use a coordinated pricing algorithm described 
in subsection A when setting rents or occupancy levels for residential dwelling units in 
the City of Berkeley.

facts.units_basis: New Jersey property class 4C (apartments, 5 or more units)

entries.explanation: Applies. New Jersey has no statewide rent control, but towns may adopt their own, and rent increases need proper written notice and cannot be unconscionable (Statewide rule: N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.1 et seq.; N.J.S.A. 2A:42-84.5). No building-based coverage test applies.
entries.title: NJ no state rent control; municipalities may adopt rent control
entries.requirement: The State of New Jersey has no laws that establish, govern or control rents, but municipalities may pass rent control or rent leveling ordinances enforced by local boards. Landlords may raise rent only by proper lease termination and written notice, the increase must not be unconscionable, and it must comply with any municipal rent control ordinance. Newly constructed multiple dwellings are exempt from local rent control for 30 years after completion of construction.
entries.key_value: No state cap; local rent control permitted; new multiple dwellings exempt 30 years
entries.quoted_span:
The State of New Jersey has no laws that establish, govern or control rents. Municipalities 
may pass an ordinance establishing rent control or rent leveling.

entries.explanation: Applies. Landlords can evict or refuse to renew a lease only for specific legal reasons and with a court order, after giving the required written notice (Statewide rule: N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.1 to 61.12).  Parcel data: at least 5 units. Exemptions ruled out by that data: Owner-occupied premises with two or fewer rental units. Not checked from parcel data: the building is not a hotel or motel; unit held in trust for developmentally disabled family member.
entries.title: NJ Anti-Eviction Act
entries.requirement: A residential landlord may remove a tenant or refuse to renew a lease only for a statutory good cause and through a court judgment for possession. Each cause except nonpayment requires a written Notice to Quit with a cause-specific period (3 days to 3 years), some causes need a prior Notice to Cease, and removal for substantial health and safety violations requires relocation assistance first.
entries.key_value: Good cause required; Notice to Quit periods from 3 days up to 3 years depending on cause; relocation assistance of 6 times monthly rent for illegal occupancy evictions
entries.quoted_span:
No residential landlord may evict or fail to renew a 
lease, whether it is a written or an oral lease without good cause.
not_checked: the building is not a hotel or motel
unit held in trust for developmentally disabled family member

entries.explanation: Applies. Landlords cannot collect a security deposit above one and a half months' rent, and yearly increases to the deposit are capped at 10% (Statewide rule: N.J.S.A. 46:8-21.2; N.J.S.A. 46:8-19; N.J.S.A. 46:8-21.1).  Parcel data: at least 5 units. Exemptions ruled out by that data: Owner-occupied two- or three-family dwelling.
entries.title: NJ Security Deposit Law
entries.requirement: A landlord may not collect a security deposit of more than one and one-half times one month's rent, and any yearly increase in the deposit may not exceed 10% of the current deposit. Prepaid rent held as security, including last month's rent, counts toward the cap, and a pet deposit cannot push the total above the cap.
entries.key_value: 1.5 x monthly rent; annual increase max 10% of current deposit
entries.quoted_span:
The maximum-security deposit to be collected by the landlord cannot be more than 
one and one-half times one month’s rent ( N.J.S.A. 46:8-21.2 ).

entries.explanation: Applies. Landlords cannot charge more than $50 (adjusted for inflation) to apply for a rental, except in one- or two-family homes (Statewide rule: N.J.S.A. 46:8-18.1).  Parcel data: at least 5 units. Exemptions ruled out by that data: One- or two-family dwelling. Not checked from parcel data: real estate licensee who is not the landlord (depends on the tenancy).
entries.title: NJ rental application fee cap
entries.requirement: A landlord or agent may not require an application or similar fee to apply to lease or sublease a residential rental property that exceeds $50, adjusted annually for CPI increases. Violators face penalties of up to $500 (first), $750 (second) and $1,000 (subsequent offenses), and the amount wrongfully charged is remitted to the applicant.
entries.key_value: $50 cap (CPI-adjusted annually)
entries.quoted_span:
A landlord, or
agent thereof, shall not require an application or other similar fee to apply
to lease or sublease a residential rental property for dwelling purposes, which
exceeds $50.
not_checked: real estate licensee who is not the landlord (depends on the tenancy)

entries.explanation: Applies. Landlords cannot ask about or use an applicant's criminal record until after a conditional offer, and then only limited convictions with an individual review (Statewide rule: N.J.S.A. 46:8-52 et seq.).  Parcel data: at least 5 units. Exemptions ruled out by that data: Owner-occupied premises of not more than four units.
entries.title: NJ Fair Chance in Housing Act
entries.requirement: Housing providers may not ask about or consider an applicant's criminal record before making a conditional offer. After a conditional offer, only certain convictions within set look-back periods may be considered, subject to an individualized assessment, written notice of withdrawal, and an appeal opportunity. Providers also may not require drug or alcohol tests of applicants.
entries.key_value: No criminal-record inquiry before conditional offer; look-back 6 years (1st degree), 4 years (2nd/3rd degree), 1 year (4th degree); serious listed offenses and lifetime sex-offender registration have no look-back limit
entries.quoted_span:
A housing
provider
shall not make any oral or written inquiry
regarding an applicant’s criminal record prior to making a conditional offer.

entries.explanation: Applies. Landlords cannot refuse to rent because of an applicant's lawful income source, but may still turn down applicants for too little income or bad credit (Statewide rule: N.J.S.A. 10:5-12; New Jersey Law Against Discrimination (N.J.S.A. 10:5-1 et seq.)).  Parcel data: at least 5 units. Exemptions ruled out by that data: Two-family owner-occupied dwelling; Room in owner- or resident-occupied single home.
entries.title: NJ Law Against Discrimination source-of-income ban
entries.citation: N.J.S.A. 10:5-12; New Jersey Law Against Discrimination (N.J.S.A. 10:5-1 et seq.)
entries.requirement: The New Jersey Law Against Discrimination requires equal treatment in renting housing regardless of listed characteristics, including source of lawful income. A landlord may still refuse to rent for insufficient income or poor credit history.
entries.key_value: Source of lawful income is a protected class
entries.quoted_span:
prohibits discrimination when selling or renting property and requires 
equal treatment in the sale or rental of housing regardless of race, creed, color, national origin,

entries.explanation: Not yet effective. Rental owners and software coordinators cannot use algorithms that pool competitors' data to coordinate rent prices, and breaking this counts as an antitrust violation (Statewide rule: P.L. 2026, c.43 (C.56:9-20 to 56:9-26)). It takes effect 2027-07-01; the as-of date is 2026-10-01.
entries.title: NJ FAIR Act algorithmic rent-setting ban
entries.requirement: It is unlawful for rental property owners to pay for or use a coordinator's services, for coordinators to perform a coordinating function or facilitate agreements restricting competition, and for any persons to engage in or facilitate parallel pricing coordination through algorithmic pricing. Violations are treated as violations of the New Jersey Antitrust Act, and municipalities may not enact conflicting ordinances.
entries.key_value: Bans use or operation of algorithmic rent-setting that pools competitively sensitive information or sets parallel prices

entries.explanation: Applies. Newark rent increases at lease renewal are limited to the inflation change and never more than 4%, with 30 days' written notice (Newark, NJ rule: Newark Rev. Gen. Ords. ch. 19:2). No building-based coverage test applies. Not checked from parcel data: public housing; the building is not a hotel or motel; the building is not a commercial.
entries.title: Newark Rent Control Ordinance
entries.requirement: At lease expiration or termination of a periodic tenancy, a landlord may not request or receive an increase greater than the CPI percentage change (CPI-U NY-NJ-Long Island, from 15 months prior to 3 months prior to the month of the proposed increase), and in no case more than 4%. Increases are barred if the dwelling is not in substantial compliance or the landlord has not registered, and require 30 days' written notice to the tenant and the Rent Regulation Officer.
entries.key_value: CPI-U change, max 4%
entries.quoted_span: no landlord may request or receive an increase greater than the percentage increase in the Consumer Price Index (CPI) from the CPI 15 months prior to the month of the proposed rent increase to the CPI three months prior to the month of the proposed rent increase. In no case shall the allowable rent increase exceed 4%.

entries.explanation: Applies. Newark defines an unconscionable rent increase as unreasonably harsh, above the landlord's cost increase, and out of line with similar rents (Newark, NJ rule: Newark Municipal Code § 2:10-11.1). No building-based coverage test applies. Not checked from parcel data: exempt from rent control under N.J.S.A. 2A:42-84.1-84.6 or HUD-controlled.
entries.title: Newark unconscionable rent increase ordinance
entries.requirement: Newark defines an 'unconscionable rent' increase for residential rental properties as one that is exceedingly harsh or unreasonable, exceeds the increase in the landlord's expenses, and is not comparable to rents at similar properties. For properties under a redevelopment or financial agreement, rent above the approved pro-forma is per se unconscionable.
entries.key_value: Rent above approved pro-forma is per se unconscionable
entries.quoted_span: Shall mean any rental increase for residential properties including but not limited to market and unsubsidized units, whose rental increases are exceedingly harsh or unreasonable that exceed the increase in the landlord’s expenses; and is not comparable to rents charged at similar properties.
not_checked: exempt from rent control under N.J.S.A. 2A:42-84.1-84.6 or HUD-controlled

entries.explanation: Applies. Newark landlords cannot try to evict a tenant as payback for the tenant using rights under the rent control law (Newark, NJ rule: Newark Rev. Gen. Ords. § 19:2-14). Covered by Newark Rev. Gen. Ords. ch. 19:2 (r-0047).
entries.title: Newark retaliatory eviction prohibition
entries.requirement: A landlord may not bring an action to recover possession of a dwelling unit as a reprisal for the tenant's efforts to secure or enforce any right under the rent control chapter.
entries.quoted_span: No landlord shall bring any action to recover possession of a dwelling unit as a reprisal for the tenant's efforts to secure or enforce any right under this chapter.

entries.explanation: Applies. Newark landlords may check criminal history only after a formal application and consent, with limited look-back periods, and must give written reasons if denying (Newark, NJ rule: Newark Municipal Code §§ 2:31-2 to 2:31-9).  Parcel data: at least 5 units. Exemptions ruled out by that data: Apartment in an owner-occupied two-family dwelling; Room rental in an owner-occupied one-family dwelling. Not checked from parcel data: government program housing for people with criminal histories.
entries.title: Newark Ban the Box rental screening
entries.requirement: Landlords and brokers may inquire into criminal history only after a formal application and written notice and consent, may look back only 8 years for indictable convictions and 5 years for disorderly persons/ordinance convictions (certain serious offenses at any time), may not use non-pending arrests, expunged/sealed records or juvenile adjudications, must weigh rehabilitation factors, and must give written reasons and the results within 10 business days of an adverse decision.
entries.key_value: Lookback: 8 years (indictable), 5 years (disorderly persons/ordinance); after formal application only
entries.quoted_span: Inquiry into and consideration of any applicant's criminal history shall take place only after the applicant has submitted a formal application.

entries.explanation: Applies. Landlords generally cannot take more than one month's rent as a deposit (two for small landlords) and must return it with an itemized list within 21 days (Statewide rule: Cal. Civ. Code § 1950.5). No building-based coverage test applies.
entries.title: California security deposit cap and return rules
entries.requirement: A landlord may not demand or receive security exceeding one month's rent (two months' rent for small natural-person landlords owning no more than two properties with four units total, except when the tenant is a service member), and must return the deposit with an itemized statement within 21 calendar days after the tenant vacates. Security cannot be labeled nonrefundable, and bad-faith retention can bring statutory damages of up to twice the deposit.
entries.key_value: One month's rent cap (two months for small landlords); 21-day return deadline
entries.quoted_span: a landlord shall not demand or receive security, however denominated, in an amount or value in excess of an amount equal to one month’s rent, in addition to any rent for the first month paid on or before initial occupancy.

entries.explanation: Applies. Landlords can charge only actual screening costs, never over $30 (adjusted for inflation), and must give an itemized receipt (Statewide rule: Cal. Civ. Code § 1950.6). No building-based coverage test applies.
entries.title: California application screening fee limits
entries.requirement: A landlord may charge an application screening fee only up to actual out-of-pocket costs and the reasonable value of time spent, never more than $30 per applicant (adjustable annually with CPI since 1998), and may not charge it when no unit is or will soon be available. The landlord must either consider applications in order and approve the first qualified applicant (charging only when an application is actually considered), or refund the full fee within 7 days of selecting a tenant or 30 days of application, whichever is first; an itemized receipt is required.
entries.key_value: $30 per applicant, CPI-adjusted; itemized receipt required
entries.quoted_span: In no case shall the amount of the application screening fee charged by the landlord or their agent be greater than thirty dollars ($30) per applicant.

entries.explanation: Applies. Landlords cannot discriminate against applicants or tenants because of their income source, including housing vouchers (Statewide rule: California Fair Employment and Housing Act (FEHA); Cal. Gov. Code § 12955). No building-based coverage test applies.
entries.title: California FEHA housing screening limits
entries.citation: California Fair Employment and Housing Act (FEHA); Cal. Gov. Code § 12955
entries.requirement: Owners may not discriminate against or harass a person because of source of income (including Section 8 and HUD-VASH vouchers and other public assistance). Where a government rent subsidy applies, income standards must be based on the tenant's share of rent, and applicants must be allowed to offer alternative evidence of ability to pay instead of credit history; owners may still ask about the level or source of income.
entries.key_value: Source of income protected; subsidy-based income test uses tenant's portion of rent
entries.quoted_span: For the owner of any housing accommodation to discriminate against or harass any person because of the race, color, religion, sex, gender, gender identity, gender expression, sexual orientation, marital status, national origin, ancestry, familial status, source of income,

entries.explanation: Applies. It is illegal to use or sell shared pricing software built on competitors' data to coordinate prices or force others to follow its prices (Statewide rule: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 16729). No building-based coverage test applies.
entries.title: California common pricing algorithm ban
entries.requirement: It is unlawful to use or distribute a common pricing algorithm, meaning software or other technology used by two or more persons that uses competitor data to recommend, align, set or influence a price, as part of a conspiracy to restrain trade, or to coerce another person to adopt the algorithm's recommended price or term. The text is general and does not name rental housing.
entries.quoted_span: It shall be unlawful for a person to use or distribute a common pricing algorithm as part of a contract, combination in the form of a trust, or conspiracy to restrain trade or commerce in violation of this chapter.

entries.quoted_span: In no case shall the amount of the application screening fee charged by the landlord or their agent be greater than thirty dollars ($30) per applicant.

The text is general and does not name rental housing.
entries.quoted_span: It shall be unlawful for a person to use or distribute a common pricing algorithm as part of a contract, combination in the form of a trust, or conspiracy to restrain trade or commerce in violation of this chapter.

entries.explanation: Applies. New Jersey has no statewide rent control, but towns may adopt their own, and rent increases need proper written notice and cannot be unconscionable (Statewide rule: N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.1 et seq.; N.J.S.A. 2A:42-84.5). No building-based coverage test applies.
entries.title: NJ no state rent control; municipalities may adopt rent control
entries.requirement: The State of New Jersey has no laws that establish, govern or control rents, but municipalities may pass rent control or rent leveling ordinances enforced by local boards. Landlords may raise rent only by proper lease termination and written notice, the increase must not be unconscionable, and it must comply with any municipal rent control ordinance. Newly constructed multiple dwellings are exempt from local rent control for 30 years after completion of construction.
entries.key_value: No state cap; local rent control permitted; new multiple dwellings exempt 30 years
entries.quoted_span:
The State of New Jersey has no laws that establish, govern or control rents. Municipalities 
may pass an ordinance establishing rent control or rent leveling.

entries.explanation: Applies. Landlords can evict or refuse to renew a lease only for specific legal reasons and with a court order, after giving the required written notice (Statewide rule: N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.1 to 61.12).  Parcel data: at least 5 units. Exemptions ruled out by that data: Owner-occupied premises with two or fewer rental units. Not checked from parcel data: the building is not a hotel or motel; unit held in trust for developmentally disabled family member.
entries.title: NJ Anti-Eviction Act
entries.requirement: A residential landlord may remove a tenant or refuse to renew a lease only for a statutory good cause and through a court judgment for possession. Each cause except nonpayment requires a written Notice to Quit with a cause-specific period (3 days to 3 years), some causes need a prior Notice to Cease, and removal for substantial health and safety violations requires relocation assistance first.
entries.key_value: Good cause required; Notice to Quit periods from 3 days up to 3 years depending on cause; relocation assistance of 6 times monthly rent for illegal occupancy evictions
entries.quoted_span:
No residential landlord may evict or fail to renew a 
lease, whether it is a written or an oral lease without good cause.

entries.explanation: Applies. Landlords cannot collect a security deposit above one and a half months' rent, and yearly increases to the deposit are capped at 10% (Statewide rule: N.J.S.A. 46:8-21.2; N.J.S.A. 46:8-19; N.J.S.A. 46:8-21.1).  Parcel data: at least 5 units. Exemptions ruled out by that data: Owner-occupied two- or three-family dwelling.
entries.title: NJ Security Deposit Law
entries.requirement: A landlord may not collect a security deposit of more than one and one-half times one month's rent, and any yearly increase in the deposit may not exceed 10% of the current deposit. Prepaid rent held as security, including last month's rent, counts toward the cap, and a pet deposit cannot push the total above the cap.
entries.key_value: 1.5 x monthly rent; annual increase max 10% of current deposit
entries.quoted_span:
The maximum-security deposit to be collected by the landlord cannot be more than 
one and one-half times one month’s rent ( N.J.S.A. 46:8-21.2 ).

entries.explanation: Applies. Landlords cannot charge more than $50 (adjusted for inflation) to apply for a rental, except in one- or two-family homes (Statewide rule: N.J.S.A. 46:8-18.1). entries.explanation: Applies. After a conditional offer, only certain convictions within set look-back periods may be considered, subject to an individualized assessment, written notice of withdrawal, and an appeal opportunity. Providers also may not require drug or alcohol tests of applicants.

entries.explanation: Applies. Landlords generally cannot take more than one month's rent as a deposit (two for small landlords) and must return it with an itemized list within 21 days (Statewide rule: Cal. Civ. Code § 1950.5). No building-based coverage test applies.
entries.title: California security deposit cap and return rules
entries.requirement: A landlord may not demand or receive security exceeding one month's rent (two months' rent for small natural-person landlords owning no more than two properties with four units total, except when the tenant is a service member), and must return the deposit with an itemized statement within 21 calendar days after the tenant vacates. Security cannot be labeled nonrefundable, and bad-faith retention can bring statutory damages of up to twice the deposit.
entries.key_value: One month's rent cap (two months for small landlords); 21-day return deadline
entries.quoted_span: a landlord shall not demand or receive security, however denominated, in an amount or value in excess of an amount equal to one month’s rent, in addition to any rent for the first month paid on or before initial occupancy.

entries.explanation: Applies. Landlords can charge only actual screening costs, never over $30 (adjusted for inflation), and must give an itemized receipt (Statewide rule: Cal. Civ. Code § 1950.6). No building-based coverage test applies.
entries.title: California application screening fee limits
entries.requirement: A landlord may charge an application screening fee only up to actual out-of-pocket costs and the reasonable value of time spent, never more than $30 per applicant (adjustable annually with CPI since 1998), and may not charge it when no unit is or will soon be available. The landlord must either consider applications in order and approve the first qualified applicant (charging only when an application is actually considered), or refund the full fee within 7 days of selecting a tenant or 30 days of application, whichever is first; an itemized receipt is required.
entries.key_value: $30 per applicant, CPI-adjusted; itemized receipt required
entries.quoted_span: In no case shall the amount of the application screening fee charged by the landlord or their agent be greater than thirty dollars ($30) per applicant.

entries.title: Berkeley rent stabilization and annual general adjustment
entries.citation: Berkeley Rent Stabilization Ordinance (Measure BB); Berkeley Municipal Code § 13.76.110(A)
entries.requirement: Landlords of fully covered units may raise rent each year only by the Annual General Adjustment set by the Rent Board using a CPI-based formula, and Measure BB caps the AGA at 5% even if the formula yields more. entries.title: Berkeley relocation assistance for owner move-in and Ellis Act evictions
entries.citation: Berkeley Rent Stabilization and Good Cause for Eviction Ordinance; Berkeley Ellis Implementation Ordinance
entries.requirement: Owners must pay tenants relocation assistance when evicting for an owner move-in or to withdraw a unit from the rental market under the Ellis Act. The payment amounts are indexed to inflation and adjusted each year by the Rent Board.

entries.quoted_span:
The landlord tells you they don't accept rental assistance. This includes Section
8 vouchers, social security disability vouchers, and veterans vouchers.

entries.explanation: Applies. New Jersey has no statewide rent control, but towns may adopt their own, and rent increases need proper written notice and cannot be unconscionable (Statewide rule: N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.1 et seq.; N.J.S.A. 2A:42-84.5). No building-based coverage test applies.
entries.title: NJ no state rent control; municipalities may adopt rent control
entries.requirement: The State of New Jersey has no laws that establish, govern or control rents, but municipalities may pass rent control or rent leveling ordinances enforced by local boards. Landlords may raise rent only by proper lease termination and written notice, the increase must not be unconscionable, and it must comply with any municipal rent control ordinance. Newly constructed multiple dwellings are exempt from local rent control for 30 years after completion of construction.
entries.key_value: No state cap; local rent control permitted; new multiple dwellings exempt 30 years
entries.quoted_span:
The State of New Jersey has no laws that establish, govern or control rents. Municipalities 
may pass an ordinance establishing rent control or rent leveling.

entries.explanation: Applies. Landlords can evict or refuse to renew a lease only for specific legal reasons and with a court order, after giving the required written notice (Statewide rule: N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.1 to 61.12).  Parcel data: at least 5 units. Exemptions ruled out by that data: Owner-occupied premises with two or fewer rental units. Not checked from parcel data: the building is not a hotel or motel; unit held in trust for developmentally disabled family member.
entries.title: NJ Anti-Eviction Act
entries.requirement: A residential landlord may remove a tenant or refuse to renew a lease only for a statutory good cause and through a court judgment for possession. Each cause except nonpayment requires a written Notice to Quit with a cause-specific period (3 days to 3 years), some causes need a prior Notice to Cease, and removal for substantial health and safety violations requires relocation assistance first.
entries.key_value: Good cause required; Notice to Quit periods from 3 days up to 3 years depending on cause; relocation assistance of 6 times monthly rent for illegal occupancy evictions
entries.quoted_span:
No residential landlord may evict or fail to renew a 
lease, whether it is a written or an oral lease without good cause.
not_checked: the building is not a hotel or motel
unit held in trust for developmentally disabled family member

entries.explanation: Applies. Landlords cannot collect a security deposit above one and a half months' rent, and yearly increases to the deposit are capped at 10% (Statewide rule: N.J.S.A. 46:8-21.2; N.J.S.A. 46:8-19; N.J.S.A. 46:8-21.1).  Parcel data: at least 5 units. Exemptions ruled out by that data: Owner-occupied two- or three-family dwelling.
entries.title: NJ Security Deposit Law
entries.requirement: A landlord may not collect a security deposit of more than one and one-half times one month's rent, and any yearly increase in the deposit may not exceed 10% of the current deposit. Prepaid rent held as security, including last month's rent, counts toward the cap, and a pet deposit cannot push the total above the cap.
entries.key_value: 1.5 x monthly rent; annual increase max 10% of current deposit
entries.quoted_span:
The maximum-security deposit to be collected by the landlord cannot be more than 
one and one-half times one month’s rent ( N.J.S.A. 46:8-21.2 ).

entries.explanation: Applies. Landlords cannot charge more than $50 (adjusted for inflation) to apply for a rental, except in one- or two-family homes (Statewide rule: N.J.S.A. 46:8-18.1).  Parcel data: at least 5 units. Exemptions ruled out by that data: One- or two-family dwelling. Not checked from parcel data: real estate licensee who is not the landlord (depends on the tenancy).
entries.title: NJ rental application fee cap
entries.requirement: A landlord or agent may not require an application or similar fee to apply to lease or sublease a residential rental property that exceeds $50, adjusted annually for CPI increases. Violators face penalties of up to $500 (first), $750 (second) and $1,000 (subsequent offenses), and the amount wrongfully charged is remitted to the applicant.
entries.key_value: $50 cap (CPI-adjusted annually)
entries.quoted_span:
A landlord, or
agent thereof, shall not require an application or other similar fee to apply
to lease or sublease a residential rental property for dwelling purposes, which
exceeds $50.

entries.explanation: Applies. Landlords cannot ask about or use an applicant's criminal record until after a conditional offer, and then only limited convictions with an individual review (Statewide rule: N.J.S.A. 46:8-52 et seq.).  Parcel data: at least 5 units. Exemptions ruled out by that data: Owner-occupied premises of not more than four units.
entries.title: NJ Fair Chance in Housing Act
entries.requirement: Housing providers may not ask about or consider an applicant's criminal record before making a conditional offer. After a conditional offer, only certain convictions within set look-back periods may be considered, subject to an individualized assessment, written notice of withdrawal, and an appeal opportunity. Providers also may not require drug or alcohol tests of applicants.
entries.key_value: No criminal-record inquiry before conditional offer; look-back 6 years (1st degree), 4 years (2nd/3rd degree), 1 year (4th degree); serious listed offenses and lifetime sex-offender registration have no look-back limit
entries.quoted_span:
A housing
provider
shall not make any oral or written inquiry
regarding an applicant’s criminal record prior to making a conditional offer.

Parcel data: at least 5 units. Exemptions ruled out by that data: Two-family owner-occupied dwelling; Room in owner- or resident-occupied single home.
entries.title: NJ Law Against Discrimination source-of-income ban
entries.citation: N.J.S.A. 10:5-12; New Jersey Law Against Discrimination (N.J.S.A. 10:5-1 et seq.)
entries.requirement: The New Jersey Law Against Discrimination requires equal treatment in renting housing regardless of listed characteristics, including source of lawful income. A landlord may still refuse to rent for insufficient income or poor credit history.
entries.key_value: Source of lawful income is a protected class

prohibits discrimination when selling or renting property and requires 
equal treatment in the sale or rental of housing regardless of race, creed, color, national origin,

Rental owners and software coordinators cannot use algorithms that pool competitors' data to coordinate rent prices, and breaking this counts as an antitrust violation (Statewide rule: P.L. 2026, c.43 (C.56:9-20 to 56:9-26)). entries.title: NJ FAIR Act algorithmic rent-setting ban
entries.requirement: It is unlawful for rental property owners to pay for or use a coordinator's services, for coordinators to perform a coordinating function or facilitate agreements restricting competition, and for any persons to engage in or facilitate parallel pricing coordination through algorithmic pricing. Violations are treated as violations of the New Jersey Antitrust Act, and municipalities may not enact conflicting ordinances.

entries.title: Hoboken rent control
entries.requirement: Rents in covered dwellings are controlled at the base rent received on October 1, 1985. At lease expiration or termination of a periodic tenancy, a landlord may not raise rent by more than the lesser of 5% or the CPI change. Only one cost-of-living increase is permitted in any twelve-month period, increases require 30 days' written notice, and increases beyond those allowed are void and refundable. Separate board-approved surcharges (taxes, water/sewer, capital improvements) and hardship increases are also available.

entries.explanation: Applies. Landlords generally cannot take more than one month's rent as a deposit (two for small landlords) and must return it with an itemized list within 21 days (Statewide rule: Cal. Civ. Code § 1950.5). No building-based coverage test applies.
entries.title: California security deposit cap and return rules
entries.requirement: A landlord may not demand or receive security exceeding one month's rent (two months' rent for small natural-person landlords owning no more than two properties with four units total, except when the tenant is a service member), and must return the deposit with an itemized statement within 21 calendar days after the tenant vacates. Security cannot be labeled nonrefundable, and bad-faith retention can bring statutory damages of up to twice the deposit.

entries.explanation: Applies. Landlords can charge only actual screening costs, never over $30 (adjusted for inflation), and must give an itemized receipt (Statewide rule: Cal. Civ. Code § 1950.6). No building-based coverage test applies.
entries.title: California application screening fee limits
entries.requirement: A landlord may charge an application screening fee only up to actual out-of-pocket costs and the reasonable value of time spent, never more than $30 per applicant (adjustable annually with CPI since 1998), and may not charge it when no unit is or will soon be available. The landlord must either consider applications in order and approve the first qualified applicant (charging only when an application is actually considered), or refund the full fee within 7 days of selecting a tenant or 30 days of application, whichever is first; an itemized receipt is required.
entries.key_value: $30 per applicant, CPI-adjusted; itemized receipt required
entries.quoted_span: In no case shall the amount of the application screening fee charged by the landlord or their agent be greater than thirty dollars ($30) per applicant.

entries.explanation: Applies. Landlords generally cannot take more than one month's rent as a deposit (two for small landlords) and must return it with an itemized list within 21 days (Statewide rule: Cal. Civ. Code § 1950.5). No building-based coverage test applies.

entries.explanation: Applies. New Jersey has no statewide rent control, but towns may adopt their own, and rent increases need proper written notice and cannot be unconscionable (Statewide rule: N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.1 et seq.; N.J.S.A. 2A:42-84.5). No building-based coverage test applies.

entries.explanation: Applies. New Jersey has no statewide rent control, but towns may adopt their own, and rent increases need proper written notice and cannot be unconscionable (Statewide rule: N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.1 et seq.; N.J.S.A. 2A:42-84.5). No building-based coverage test applies.
entries.title: NJ no state rent control; municipalities may adopt rent control
entries.requirement: The State of New Jersey has no laws that establish, govern or control rents, but municipalities may pass rent control or rent leveling ordinances enforced by local boards. Landlords may raise rent only by proper lease termination and written notice, the increase must not be unconscionable, and it must comply with any municipal rent control ordinance. Newly constructed multiple dwellings are exempt from local rent control for 30 years after completion of construction.
entries.key_value: No state cap; local rent control permitted; new multiple dwellings exempt 30 years
entries.quoted_span:
The State of New Jersey has no laws that establish, govern or control rents. Municipalities 
may pass an ordinance establishing rent control or rent leveling.

entries.key_value: One month's rent cap (two months for small landlords); 21-day return deadline
entries.quoted_span: a landlord shall not demand or receive security, however denominated, in an amount or value in excess of an amount equal to one month’s rent, in addition to any rent for the first month paid on or before initial occupancy.

entries.explanation: Applies. Landlords can charge only actual screening costs, never over $30 (adjusted for inflation), and must give an itemized receipt (Statewide rule: Cal. Civ. Code § 1950.6). No building-based coverage test applies.
entries.title: California application screening fee limits
entries.requirement: A landlord may charge an application screening fee only up to actual out-of-pocket costs and the reasonable value of time spent, never more than $30 per applicant (adjustable annually with CPI since 1998), and may not charge it when no unit is or will soon be available. The landlord must either consider applications in order and approve the first qualified applicant (charging only when an application is actually considered), or refund the full fee within 7 days of selecting a tenant or 30 days of application, whichever is first; an itemized receipt is required.
entries.key_value: $30 per applicant, CPI-adjusted; itemized receipt required
entries.quoted_span: In no case shall the amount of the application screening fee charged by the landlord or their agent be greater than thirty dollars ($30) per applicant.

entries.explanation: Applies. Landlords cannot discriminate against applicants or tenants because of their income source, including housing vouchers (Statewide rule: California Fair Employment and Housing Act (FEHA); Cal. Gov. Code § 12955). No building-based coverage test applies.

entries.explanation: Applies. It is illegal to use or sell shared pricing software built on competitors' data to coordinate prices or force others to follow its prices (Statewide rule: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 16729). No building-based coverage test applies.
entries.title: California common pricing algorithm ban

The text is general and does not name rental housing.
entries.quoted_span: It shall be unlawful for a person to use or distribute a common pricing algorithm as part of a contract, combination in the form of a trust, or conspiracy to restrain trade or commerce in violation of this chapter.

entries.explanation: Applies. entries.explanation: Applies. A rental broker can work for the tenant or the landlord but not both, and only the party who hired the broker pays the fee (Statewide rule: G.L. c. 112 § 87DDD1/2). No building-based coverage test applies.

entries.quoted_span: Any fee shall only be paid by the party, lessor or tenant who originally engaged and entered into a contract with the licensed broker or salesperson.

entries.explanation: Applies. New Jersey has no statewide rent control, but towns may adopt their own, and rent increases need proper written notice and cannot be unconscionable (Statewide rule: N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.1 et seq.; N.J.S.A. 2A:42-84.5). No building-based coverage test applies.
entries.title: NJ no state rent control; municipalities may adopt rent control

Landlords may raise rent only by proper lease termination and written notice, the increase must not be unconscionable, and it must comply with any municipal rent control ordinance. Newly constructed multiple dwellings are exempt from local rent control for 30 years after completion of construction.
entries.key_value: No state cap; local rent control permitted; new multiple dwellings exempt 30 years
entries.quoted_span:
The State of New Jersey has no laws that establish, govern or control rents. Municipalities 
may pass an ordinance establishing rent control or rent leveling.

entries.explanation: Applies. Landlords cannot charge more than $50 (adjusted for inflation) to apply for a rental, except in one- or two-family homes (Statewide rule: N.J.S.A. 46:8-18.1). entries.explanation: Applies. New Jersey has no statewide rent control, but towns may adopt their own, and rent increases need proper written notice and cannot be unconscionable (Statewide rule: N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.1 et seq.; N.J.S.A. 2A:42-84.5). No building-based coverage test applies.

Newly constructed multiple dwellings are exempt from local rent control for 30 years after completion of construction.

entries.quoted_span:

entries.explanation: Applies. In San Francisco it is illegal to sell or use software that uses competitors' private data to set rents for residential units (San Francisco, CA rule: S.F. Admin. Code § 37.10C). No building-based coverage test applies.

entries.explanation: Applies. Landlords generally cannot take more than one month's rent as a deposit (two for small landlords) and must return it with an itemized list within 21 days (Statewide rule: Cal. Civ. Code § 1950.5). No building-based coverage test applies.
entries.title: California security deposit cap and return rules
entries.requirement: A landlord may not demand or receive security exceeding one month's rent (two months' rent for small natural-person landlords owning no more than two properties with four units total, except when the tenant is a service member), and must return the deposit with an itemized statement within 21 calendar days after the tenant vacates. Security cannot be labeled nonrefundable, and bad-faith retention can bring statutory damages of up to twice the deposit.

entries.quoted_span: a landlord shall not demand or receive security, however denominated, in an amount or value in excess of an amount equal to one month’s rent, in addition to any rent for the first month paid on or before initial occupancy.

entries.explanation: Applies. Landlords can charge only actual screening costs, never over $30 (adjusted for inflation), and must give an itemized receipt (Statewide rule: Cal. Civ. Code § 1950.6). No building-based coverage test applies.
entries.title: California application screening fee limits
entries.requirement: A landlord may charge an application screening fee only up to actual out-of-pocket costs and the reasonable value of time spent, never more than $30 per applicant (adjustable annually with CPI since 1998), and may not charge it when no unit is or will soon be available. entries.key_value: $30 per applicant, CPI-adjusted; itemized receipt required
entries.quoted_span: In no case shall the amount of the application screening fee charged by the landlord or their agent be greater than thirty dollars ($30) per applicant.

entries.key_value: No discrimination against public assistance or housing subsidy recipients (including rental assistance)
entries.quoted_span: For any person furnishing credit, services or rental accommodations to discriminate against any individual who is a recipient of federal, state, or local public assistance, including medical assistance, or who is a tenant receiving federal, state, or local housing subsidies, including rental assistance or rental supplements,

entries.explanation: Applies. Cambridge landlords cannot discriminate based on source of income, including Section 8, and must apply tenant selection standards equally to everyone (Cambridge, MA rule: Cambridge Municipal Code ch. 14.04).  Parcel data: built 1910, 6 units. Exemptions ruled out by that data: Owner-occupied 2-family dwelling.
entries.title: Cambridge Fair Housing Ordinance
entries.requirement: Source of income, including Section 8 and public benefits, is a protected category under the Cambridge Fair Housing Ordinance, so landlords cannot discriminate against applicants on that basis. Landlords and rental agents may use any reasonable tenant selection standard (such as ability to pay rent and to care for the apartment) if it is applied equally and uniformly to all applicants.
entries.key_value: Source of income (incl. Section 8 and public benefits) is a protected category
entries.quoted_span: Under the law, landlords, sellers and rental agents may use any reasonable standard to determine which applicants are selected, as long as that standard is applied equally and uniformly to all applicants.

entries.requirement: After a tenant has continuously and lawfully occupied a unit for 12 months, the owner may terminate the tenancy only for stated at-fault or no-fault just cause. entries.explanation: Applies. Landlords generally cannot take more than one month's rent as a deposit (two for small landlords) and must return it with an itemized list within 21 days (Statewide rule: Cal. Civ. Code § 1950.5). No building-based coverage test applies.
entries.title: California security deposit cap and return rules
entries.requirement: A landlord may not demand or receive security exceeding one month's rent (two months' rent for small natural-person landlords owning no more than two properties with four units total, except when the tenant is a service member), and must return the deposit with an itemized statement within 21 calendar days after the tenant vacates. Security cannot be labeled nonrefundable, and bad-faith retention can bring statutory damages of up to twice the deposit.
entries.key_value: One month's rent cap (two months for small landlords); 21-day return deadline
entries.quoted_span: a landlord shall not demand or receive security, however denominated, in an amount or value in excess of an amount equal to one month’s rent, in addition to any rent for the first month paid on or before initial occupancy.

entries.explanation: Applies. Landlords can charge only actual screening costs, never over $30 (adjusted for inflation), and must give an itemized receipt (Statewide rule: Cal. Civ. Code § 1950.6). No building-based coverage test applies.
entries.title: California application screening fee limits
entries.requirement: A landlord may charge an application screening fee only up to actual out-of-pocket costs and the reasonable value of time spent, never more than $30 per applicant (adjustable annually with CPI since 1998), and may not charge it when no unit is or will soon be available. The landlord must either consider applications in order and approve the first qualified applicant (charging only when an application is actually considered), or refund the full fee within 7 days of selecting a tenant or 30 days of application, whichever is first; an itemized receipt is required.
entries.key_value: $30 per applicant, CPI-adjusted; itemized receipt required
entries.quoted_span: In no case shall the amount of the application screening fee charged by the landlord or their agent be greater than thirty dollars ($30) per applicant.

entries.explanation: Applies. Landlords cannot discriminate against applicants or tenants because of their income source, including housing vouchers (Statewide rule: California Fair Employment and Housing Act (FEHA); Cal. Gov. Code § 12955). No building-based coverage test applies.
entries.title: California FEHA housing screening limits
entries.citation: California Fair Employment and Housing Act (FEHA); Cal. Gov. Code § 12955
entries.requirement: Owners may not discriminate against or harass a person because of source of income (including Section 8 and HUD-VASH vouchers and other public assistance). Where a government rent subsidy applies, income standards must be based on the tenant's share of rent, and applicants must be allowed to offer alternative evidence of ability to pay instead of credit history; owners may still ask about the level or source of income.
entries.key_value: Source of income protected; subsidy-based income test uses tenant's portion of rent
entries.quoted_span: For the owner of any housing accommodation to discriminate against or harass any person because of the race, color, religion, sex, gender, gender identity, gender expression, sexual orientation, marital status, national origin, ancestry, familial status, source of income,

entries.explanation: Applies. It is illegal to use or sell shared pricing software built on competitors' data to coordinate prices or force others to follow its prices (Statewide rule: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 16729). No building-based coverage test applies.
entries.title: California common pricing algorithm ban
entries.requirement: It is unlawful to use or distribute a common pricing algorithm, meaning software or other technology used by two or more persons that uses competitor data to recommend, align, set or influence a price, as part of a conspiracy to restrain trade, or to coerce another person to adopt the algorithm's recommended price or term. The text is general and does not name rental housing.
entries.quoted_span: It shall be unlawful for a person to use or distribute a common pricing algorithm as part of a contract, combination in the form of a trust, or conspiracy to restrain trade or commerce in violation of this chapter.

Coverage depends on: year built is missing in the parcel data (needed: first occupied before 1980-01-01).
entries.title: Berkeley rent stabilization and annual general adjustment
entries.citation: Berkeley Rent Stabilization Ordinance (Measure BB); Berkeley Municipal Code § 13.76.110(A)
entries.requirement: Landlords of fully covered units may raise rent each year only by the Annual General Adjustment set by the Rent Board using a CPI-based formula, and Measure BB caps the AGA at 5% even if the formula yields more. Landlords with banked AGAs may still raise rent above 5% to reach the rent ceiling.
entries.key_value: CPI-based AGA, max 5%
entries.quoted_span: The maximum AGA is 5%. This means that, if the formula in the Rent Ordinance results in an AGA that is greater than 5%, the AGA approved by the Board for that year can be no more than 5%.

entries.explanation: Applies. Berkeley owners must pay tenants relocation money when evicting for owner move-in or to take a unit off the rental market; amounts update each year (Berkeley, CA rule: Berkeley Rent Stabilization and Good Cause for Eviction Ordinance; Berkeley Ellis Implementation Ordinance). No building-based coverage test applies. Applies to tenancies where: evicted for owner move-in or Ellis Act withdrawal.
entries.title: Berkeley relocation assistance for owner move-in and Ellis Act evictions
entries.citation: Berkeley Rent Stabilization and Good Cause for Eviction Ordinance; Berkeley Ellis Implementation Ordinance
entries.requirement: Owners must pay tenants relocation assistance when evicting for an owner move-in or to withdraw a unit from the rental market under the Ellis Act. The payment amounts are indexed to inflation and adjusted each year by the Rent Board.
entries.key_value: Standard payment $19,413; additional payment for qualifying households $6,471 (effective 2026-01-01; 1.5% CPI adjustment)
entries.quoted_span: The Rent Stabilization and Good Cause for Eviction Ordinance requires owners to pay tenants relocation assistance in the event of an owner move-in eviction.

entries.explanation: Unknown. Berkeley tenants in covered units can be evicted only for just cause, and owners cannot evict over small rental debts or for refusing a new fixed-term lease (Berkeley, CA rule: Berkeley Rent Stabilization Ordinance (as amended by Measure BB)). Coverage depends on: year built is missing in the parcel data (needed: first occupied before 1980-01-01).
entries.title: Berkeley just cause for eviction
entries.citation: Berkeley Rent Stabilization Ordinance (as amended by Measure BB)
entries.requirement: Tenants in fully or partially covered units cannot be evicted without just cause. Measure BB bars eviction for rental debt under one month of Fair Market Rent or for refusing to sign a new fixed-term lease, requires lease-breach evictions to show substantial actual harm and unreasonable tenant behavior, and requires notices to be filed with the Rent Board within three business days.
entries.key_value: Nonpayment eviction only if debt >= one month's Fair Market Rent
entries.quoted_span: In Berkeley, tenants in units that are fully or partially covered by the Rent Ordinance cannot be evicted unless there is "just cause” (previously called “good cause”).

entries.explanation: Unknown. Berkeley landlords of covered units must pay tenants interest on security deposits each year, prorated if the tenant moves out early (Berkeley, CA rule: Berkeley Rent Stabilization Ordinance). Coverage depends on: requires fully or partially covered by Berkeley Rent Ordinance, which is not in the parcel data.
entries.title: Berkeley security deposit interest requirement
entries.requirement: For tenancies in units fully or partially covered by the Berkeley Rent Ordinance, landlords must pay tenants interest on the security deposit at the end of each year, and a prorated amount if the tenant moves out before year end.
entries.key_value: Annual interest on deposit, prorated on move-out
entries.quoted_span: landlords must pay tenants interest on their security deposit at the end of each year and a prorated amount if the tenant moves out before the end of the year.

entries.explanation: Applies. Berkeley landlords must disclose tenant screening fee rights and the state fee cap, and cannot charge non-refundable renewal or roommate-change fees (Berkeley, CA rule: Berkeley Municipal Code ch. 13.78). No building-based coverage test applies.
entries.title: Berkeley screening fee disclosure ordinance
entries.requirement: Owners charging a fee for a credit report or application processing must provide a clear tenant screening fee rights statement and the state maximum fee cap before receiving the fee. Owners may not charge existing tenants a non-refundable fee for renewing a tenancy or for adding, replacing, or removing a roommate.
entries.key_value: Disclosure of Cal. Civ. Code 1950.6(b) fee cap; no non-refundable renewal or roommate fees
entries.quoted_span: An owner of residential rental property (or the owner’s agent) cannot charge a non-refundable fee to any existing tenant for the purpose of renewing a tenancy, in whole or in part,

entries.explanation: Applies. Berkeley landlords cannot ask about or use criminal history in choosing or managing tenants, and must give written notice and a chance to respond first (Berkeley, CA rule: Berkeley Municipal Code ch. 13.106).  Parcel data: at least 5 units. Exemptions ruled out by that data: Owner-occupied 1-3 unit property. Not checked from parcel data: lifetime sex offender (depends on the tenancy); public housing or Section 8 property; owner move-back rental agreement (depends on the tenancy).
entries.title: Berkeley Fair Chance Access to Housing Ordinance
entries.requirement: Rental housing providers may not ask about or use criminal history in advertising, applications, tenant selection, or tenancy decisions, and must give written notice and an opportunity to respond before taking any action based on criminal history. Violations carry administrative fines of $1,000 to $10,000 per violation plus civil damages.
entries.key_value: Criminal history inquiries and use prohibited; fines $1,000-$10,000 per violation
entries.quoted_span: The Fair Chance Access to Housing Ordinance prohibits rental housing providers in Berkeley from asking about and using criminal history and/or criminal background checks in their rental housing advertising, applications, tenant selection process, or decision-making.
not_checked: lifetime sex offender (depends on the tenancy)
public housing or Section 8 property
owner move-back rental agreement (depends on the tenancy)
existing tenant sublet or roommate change (depends on the tenancy)

entries.explanation: Applies. In Berkeley, landlords cannot use pricing software that relies on competitors' private data to set rents, with fines up to $1,000 per violation (Berkeley, CA rule: Berkeley Municipal Code ch. 13.63). No building-based coverage test applies.
entries.title: Berkeley ban on coordinated rent-pricing algorithms
entries.requirement: It is unlawful to sell, license, or provide to Berkeley landlords, or for a landlord to use, a coordinated pricing algorithm that uses non-public competitor data to set or recommend rents or occupancy levels for residential units. Each month and each unit constitutes a separate violation, with civil penalties up to $1,000 per violation plus attorney's fees.
entries.key_value: Ban on coordinated pricing algorithms; civil penalties up to $1,000 per violation
entries.quoted_span:
It shall be unlawful for a landlord to use a coordinated pricing algorithm described 
in subsection A when setting rents or occupancy levels for residential dwelling units in 
the City of Berkeley.

entries.explanation: Applies. New Jersey has no statewide rent control, but towns may adopt their own, and rent increases need proper written notice and cannot be unconscionable (Statewide rule: N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.1 et seq.; N.J.S.A. 2A:42-84.5). No building-based coverage test applies.
entries.title: NJ no state rent control; municipalities may adopt rent control
entries.requirement: The State of New Jersey has no laws that establish, govern or control rents, but municipalities may pass rent control or rent leveling ordinances enforced by local boards. Landlords may raise rent only by proper lease termination and written notice, the increase must not be unconscionable, and it must comply with any municipal rent control ordinance. Newly constructed multiple dwellings are exempt from local rent control for 30 years after completion of construction.
entries.key_value: No state cap; local rent control permitted; new multiple dwellings exempt 30 years
entries.quoted_span:

entries.explanation: Applies. entries.title: NJ Anti-Eviction Act
entries.requirement: A residential landlord may remove a tenant or refuse to renew a lease only for a statutory good cause and through a court judgment for possession. Each cause except nonpayment requires a written Notice to Quit with a cause-specific period (3 days to 3 years), some causes need a prior Notice to Cease, and removal for substantial health and safety violations requires relocation assistance first.
entries.key_value: Good cause required; Notice to Quit periods from 3 days up to 3 years depending on cause; relocation assistance of 6 times monthly rent for illegal occupancy evictions

No residential landlord may evict or fail to renew a 
lease, whether it is a written or an oral lease without good cause.

unit held in trust for developmentally disabled family member

entries.explanation: Applies. Landlords cannot collect a security deposit above one and a half months' rent, and yearly increases to the deposit are capped at 10% (Statewide rule: N.J.S.A. 46:8-21.2; N.J.S.A. 46:8-19; N.J.S.A. 46:8-21.1).  Parcel data: at least 5 units. Exemptions ruled out by that data: Owner-occupied two- or three-family dwelling.
entries.title: NJ Security Deposit Law
entries.requirement: A landlord may not collect a security deposit of more than one and one-half times one month's rent, and any yearly increase in the deposit may not exceed 10% of the current deposit. Prepaid rent held as security, including last month's rent, counts toward the cap, and a pet deposit cannot push the total above the cap.
entries.key_value: 1.5 x monthly rent; annual increase max 10% of current deposit
entries.quoted_span:
The maximum-security deposit to be collected by the landlord cannot be more than 
one and one-half times one month’s rent ( N.J.S.A. 46:8-21.2 ).

entries.explanation: Applies. Landlords cannot charge more than $50 (adjusted for inflation) to apply for a rental, except in one- or two-family homes (Statewide rule: N.J.S.A. 46:8-18.1). entries.title: NJ rental application fee cap
entries.requirement: A landlord or agent may not require an application or similar fee to apply to lease or sublease a residential rental property that exceeds $50, adjusted annually for CPI increases. Violators face penalties of up to $500 (first), $750 (second) and $1,000 (subsequent offenses), and the amount wrongfully charged is remitted to the applicant.

A landlord, or
agent thereof, shall not require an application or other similar fee to apply
to lease or sublease a residential rental property for dwelling purposes, which
exceeds $50.

entries.title: Hoboken rent control
entries.requirement: Rents in covered dwellings are controlled at the base rent received on October 1, 1985. At lease expiration or termination of a periodic tenancy, a landlord may not raise rent by more than the lesser of 5% or the CPI change. Only one cost-of-living increase is permitted in any twelve-month period, increases require 30 days' written notice, and increases beyond those allowed are void and refundable. entries.title: Massachusetts broker fee rule

entries.key_value: Fee paid only by the party who hired the broker
entries.quoted_span: Any fee shall only be paid by the party, lessor or tenant who originally engaged and entered into a contract with the licensed broker or salesperson.

entries.explanation: Applies. Landlords generally cannot take more than one month's rent as a deposit (two for small landlords) and must return it with an itemized list within 21 days (Statewide rule: Cal. Civ. Code § 1950.5). No building-based coverage test applies.
entries.title: California security deposit cap and return rules
entries.requirement: A landlord may not demand or receive security exceeding one month's rent (two months' rent for small natural-person landlords owning no more than two properties with four units total, except when the tenant is a service member), and must return the deposit with an itemized statement within 21 calendar days after the tenant vacates. entries.explanation: Applies. Landlords can charge only actual screening costs, never over $30 (adjusted for inflation), and must give an itemized receipt (Statewide rule: Cal. Civ. Code § 1950.6). No building-based coverage test applies.
entries.title: California application screening fee limits
entries.requirement: A landlord may charge an application screening fee only up to actual out-of-pocket costs and the reasonable value of time spent, never more than $30 per applicant (adjustable annually with CPI since 1998), and may not charge it when no unit is or will soon be available.
